div.p: Here teen extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Studente of the London
Hospital

"Tests a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without It. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about nye o'clock, when I get into apiece, the lady of the housa will say to me: ' Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, • I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and tills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of all Black China Ten ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the nervoos system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do. so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous dietorbanoe, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresti, get Black China Teo, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for eaeh person and one forth, blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling wAter, and within five minutes you must pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good."

Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's *pinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what tial• old fashioned ea is like. The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be fouad tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to Its apparent insipidness ; but it its use is persisted In, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system, and if, in a week to two after its use, a trial Is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement.

-- IT takes a fast man to run quickly through t. fortune. FORTUNE does not change men; it only brings out, in clear light, what's in them. AN old lady says her son will never be struck by lightning, because he always gets insulate (in so late). LUCK is a good tiling, but pluck is a better thing. One has to wait for luck, but pluck is always ready to go ahead. THE girls are making such a fuss about the correct thing in neckties that the Boston Pod calls it " a raging tie-fuss." IT is a good thing to make a sacrifice fern friend; and it is also a good thing to conceal the effort made in maliog the sacrifice. A GENIAL old professor, who was known as a very accomplished grammarian, was yet weak on one point: he could never decline a kiss. A commix lyceum lately had up for solution the conundrum: "Which is the more detestable, the grinning hypocrite, or the groaning one ?" THE ditterence between a cat confined in a bag and the wind sighing through a dilapidated house is that one cries through a sack and the other sighs through a crack. A CONCEITED fop, who was fond of talking about hiansslf, once asked Belem what was the chief rule of etiquette in social intercourse. •" Absolute silenoe in regard to yourself," replied the wit. Two Quaker girls were ironing on the Bartle table. One asked the other which she would take —the right or the left. She answered promptly: "It will be right for me to take the left, and then , it will be left for thee to take the right.";' Tus author of an epic poem asked Jerrold if he had ever seen his "Descent into Hell." "No," replied Jerrold, with a chuckle of delight; "but I should like to." WHEN some member of the Museum Club, hearing an air mentioned, exclaimed, "That always carries me away when I hear it," "Can nobody whistle it?" asked Douglas Jerrold. A SCHOOL EXAMINER asked why the sea is salt. He got three answers—one, "Because of the Yarmouth bloaters " ; one, "To keep the drovvnded folk sweet" • and one, from a pious little maiden, " Becanae God made it so." AN old fashioued minister passing a fashionable , church, not long ago, on which a new spire was going up, was asked how much higher it was to be. "Not much," he answerea ; "that congregation don't own much higher in that direction." A scuoot BOY spelt d-e-c-ion-a-1 and pronounced it (Daniel. "What do you mean by calling that dismal exobsimed the teacher. " 'Cause it is," answered the boy. "It's dismal fractions. All fractions are dinnal. There isn't a bit of fun in any of 'em." DOUGLAS JERROLD is seriously disappointed with a certain book written by one of his friends and has expressed his disappointment. Friend—"l hear you said a-- was the worst book I ever wrote.' Jerrold—" No, I didn't. I said it was the worst book anybody ever wrote." DE Bacos—" I'm a wretched man, Bagley. I am afflicted with insomnia, and life is getting to be a burden." Bagley—" Nonsense I there are plenty of cures for that." De Beggs (despairingly)— "Yes, I know there are, but I've tried them all without effect. Igo to ohurch regularly, and even there I can't eo to sleep." At a dinner parts the other evening a lady said to the gentleman next to her, "I don't know, Mr —, whether you are at all afraid of the measles. , bat my little children have them, and I have been suffering from a slight attack." The gentleman rose to the occasion. "Madam," he replied, "I should be only too delighted to take anything from no charming a source." ANGRY UNCLE (to spendthrift nephew) "You say you gave your note at thirty days for those dogs of yours, sir? Where is that note now?" .Nepkew—" In the bank, I believe." Uncle—" In the bank? What's it doing in the bank ?" Nephew —" Drawing interest, sir." A NEVADA politician was elected on the merits of a single epeech, the effect of which was described as "absolutely irresistible." All he said was: "Fellow countrymen, remember whence ye're sprung, and follow me to yonder saloon and thence to a glorious victory !" A roarrictats who was always in a quarrelsome mood, having very much annoyed a brother Senator, the latter suddenly turned upon him and asked "Why are you and a camel so much alike ?" "I give it up," was the reply. " Well," said the Senator, "it is because you both 'got your backs up' while young and have kept them so ever since." A DISTINGUISHED diplomatist from the United States of America, a very genial and social being, soon after his arrival in London made the round of the sights—Madame Tussaud's among the number "And what do you think of our waxwork !" asked a friend. " Well," replied the General, "it struck me as being very like an ordinary English party." "My Soar," said Mr. Spriggins to his little son, who was devouring an egg—it was Mr. Spriggins's desire to instruct his boy—" my son, do you know that chickens come out of eggs ?" "Do they, father ?" said the young hopeful; "I thought the reverse." The elder Spriggins drew back from the table, sadly, and gazed on his son, then put on his bat and went out. Tier Rochester (Minn.) Poet says :" The revolver Is a dangerous bird of prey. Mr. Maitland Cross was putting one into a drawer Tuesday evening, when, somehow, the hammer caught, and die- nbarged one chamber. The ball struek Maitland in the third finger of the right hand, and after ripping it open, lodged in the first joint. A doctor removed the ball, and now the wounded finger is waiking around the town, with Maitland as chief nurse." "Dealt Camara's," said Mrs. Smith, a young ee. married woman, leaning on her husband's shoulder, ~as he sat at his desk writing. " Well, what the • ra mischief do you want now ?' he growled. "Dear .t.a 'Charles, do you love me as much now as you did ,-ste when we were first married ?" "I told yen so .a-a- more than 40 times. If you ask me again I'll ao bounce a paper weight on yen. Yes I yes! yes Are you satisfied now 7" "Wm. you give me your hand?" sternly said a. ...aunty schoolmaster to a girl who had refused to hold out her hand to be feruled. As she answered not, he said "Do you refuse to give me your hand ?" "I must," she sobbed, "unless pa ooneents." She was pretty, told the old man had a hundred and sixty acres, all paid for and well stocked, and so there was no difficulty in adjusting matters. Din young folks were talking about mistskes in a% courtship when Uncle Job broke in with the declaration "that there was not any such thing, for," said he, "nobody ever makes any mistakes worth mentioning in courtship. It's after the courtship's over and the lovers have been married that the hurtful mistakes "Well, uncle," said one of his pretty nieoes, atherhatat the moral asa of all that?" "The moralla,' exclaimed Uncle o' Jab. "What's the moral a7hy, I s'pose the moral is: Keep en courtise 1" WHEN Thomas Sheridan was in a nervous debilitated condition, and dining with his father at Peter Moore's, the servant, in passing fireplace, knocked down the plate warnu made such a clatter as caused the invalid and tremble. Moore provoked by the accident, rebuked the man, and added—" I suppose you have broken all the plates ?" "No, sir," said the servant, "not one !" "Not one 1" exclaimed ' ,Sheridan; "then, d—n it, you have made all ' this noise for nothing I" ' 'WHEN the first edition of the " Seasons " out, the poet sent a copy, handsomely bound, to Sir Gilbert Elliot, of Irlinto, afterwards Lord Justice-Clerk, who had shown the poet' great kindness. Sir Gilbert showed the book to his gardener, a relation of James Thomson, who took the book into his hands, and turning it over and over and gazing on it with admiration, Sir Gilbert said to him, "Wee', David, what do you think of your friend James Thomson now? There's a book will make him famous all the world over, and inunortalke his name." David, looking now at Sir C4ifilert and then at the book, said, "lii nada sir, it is a grand book; I didne think the lad had ingenuity enough to hs.e done sic a neat piece o' hanatoraft." Mr. Gladstone's friendship with the late Mr. John Murray, extending over more than half a century, was maintained till the last. On the day after he reached London on his return from the Riviera, Mr. Gladstone hearing that his old publisher was ill, went to call upon him. He did not see him, Mr. Murray being then too ill to receive visitors.

"It is not the cowl that makes the monk," but dress goes a long way. A Welsh dean who does not always wear the imposing costume of his exalted degree in the Church, was travelling the other day in a third-class carriage. " Now, you're a curate, I suppose," said a friendly passenger, eyeing the M.B. waistcoat. " I was a curate once," saia the dean, with an accent on the adverb. "Oh, I see," returned his companion ; "drink, I suppose."

According to the latest Return, made up to the Ist of November, 1891, the maximum authorised strength of the Volunteer force was 261,214. Not less than 222,046 have been enrolled, of whom only 7.849 are returned as non-efficient. On the let of December, 1870, the maximum establishment was a fraction under 245,000; the total enrolled was 193,893, of whom 23,000 were non-efficient. Twenty years ago the percentage of efficieras to enrolled was 88.2. It is now 96.47.

Surprise is expressed that Mr. Fred Ginnett, the circus proprietor, should have left so large a for- tune as .£32,000. This is nothing out of the way for a circus proprietor. When Mr. Charles Hengler died four years ago his personal estate exceeded .£lOO,OOO, and Mr. John Sanger in the following year left .£40,747. Mr. Ginnett'a education was the rough-and-tumble training of the ring, but he was shrewd, steady, and careful, and seems to have transmitted these qualities to his sons. '

The fact that the influenza proved fatal chiefly among the well-to-do classes was noted at the time of the epidemic. Proof of this is forthcoming by consideration of the fact, attested by a high authority in the House of Commons, that whereas the Exchequer has largely benefited by probate duty paid upon wills proved within the last few months, assurance societies dealing with the middle classes show no appreciable increase of drain upon their resources, consequent upon exceptional mortality.

The Queen follows nearly the same routine at Costebello as at Balmoral. Her Majesty breakfasts alone at nine o'clock, and then works for a couplet hours (more or less) with Sir Henry Ponsonby,while [The Duke of Rutland usually has an audience in the course of the morning. At twelve o'clock the Queen goes for an " airing " in the pine woods in her i•dOnkey-chaise, and at two o'clock her Majesty lunches, in Company with Princess Beatrice. About half-past three the Queen starts in an open carriage on a two hours' drive. On returning, tea is served, and then the London newspapers of the previous day and a batch of correspondence occupy at least an hour, and several telegrams are sure to be wait- ing which require to be answered at once, and which usually involve a second sitting with St. Henry Pon- sonby. The Queen dines between half-past eight and a quarter to nine, and the suite take their meal at the same hour in another room: Her Majesty reads, or converses with Princess Beatrice and Lady Churchill, after dinner; and she retires to bed about eleven o'clock. ,ot I rs:'t

Bv H. WHITHAM. Yes, the old rule must have its innings once more. I thought of writing under a caption—such as " The survival of the fittest," but a thought seemed to pass through my mind that the phrase, true in itself, was none the less misleading. I don't think I should be the fittest man for pick and shovel work on your Ship Canal, or that Sir Gilbert Greenell would have made a first class temperance advocate. No, I feel quite sure we should both have failed, and ahould have gone under, thus, giving place to the fittest men to do the work they were fitted for. I was led into this train of thought through reading in the colums of a Warrington paper, an article headed "Destitute Returned Emigrants." I have been a Radical all my life, and have formed very definite ideas as to what goes towards the making of a patriot, and when I finished reading the article , referred to, I said to myself, "thousands of acres of I good English land, all lying idle, yet not an acre for an English born man. Land, land, everywhere, yet not a bit to till." With Tolstoi, I cried out, WHAT'S TO BE DONE r and the answer came, "Back to the land." You may scratch the Tory until he has parted with the last drop of blood ; yc,u won't even then have reached the patriot. If it is a case of handing down to posterity a national debt, you will find the Jingo— "that, and nothing more." But what of this tale of destitute emigrants? I know the sort of country these poor emigrants were pitchforked into, and the sort of people they would be" handled" by,and, when I read the story, my agitation Was intense. To think that this was all that England could do for her sons and daughters was to me a bitter grief—you will understand its intensity before fin- ishing this letter. This poor emigrant, telling hie tale, says he got work, after sleeping on the beach for live weeks, at 2s. Id. per day, his wife the same. They could not live on this. "The work was so bad and the wages so small that we could not do it, and we went to Bahia and appealed to the British Consul. lie was a very kind gentleman, and kindly listened to our sorrowful tale. But he told us Lord Salisbury had sent word to say that the Consuls were to do nothing whatever for the emigrants." You who love your country, you who claim tor your countrymen the right to live, remember Lord Salis- bury's words,quoted by a Tory journal, "Do nothing whatever for the emigrants.' He, like the German Emperor, would bid those who don't like the coun- try to leave it. I have read within the past few months qaite a number of reports of meetings held to consider what should be done with your surplus population, and from "General " Booth upwards there seems to prevail one idea, viz.—that, in emi- gration lies the secret of England's tranquillity. A greater fallacy was never promulgated, nay, sir, a greater crime cannot be committed than to send men and women away from their native land, with- out question as to their fitness for pioneer work, or as to the honest demand for such labour as may form the emigrant's capital. Since writing the above I have managed to run a piece of copper through my right hand, so that lam off work again, with • SWOLLEN AND POISONED HAND. Doing ray best to write this letter, with the sun shining in the window, I feel as if I would, with Ruskin" do what I can for the help of my coun- try and its honour." Yes, the sun does shine on us all alike, the just and the unjust. That is a true saying, and it passes the wit of man to understand why the unjust should so abound, and the fair face of this earth should be scared with such numberless blotches of misery. Possibly some of my readers may think me lost in the deepest depths of pessim- ism. If so, they would be wrong. lam optimistic to the core, but I would make it practical. If Christianity is optimistic, let us see it made practi- cal, and then life will be worth living in this best of all possible worlds. For a great number of years my writings have had a Socialistic tendency, yet I could never be a Socialist. My loVe of liberty, is too great for me to ever place myself under State control. The largest and most prosperous Nationa- list Club on the Pacific Slope is the one which I was the means of starting, and of Which I was the first President, yet I had to leave it on account of its too great love for Bellamy and his State control ideas. I believe that everything may be gained for the people,by the .people, so soon as the people are clear as to their wants. The real wants of the peo- ple are few and should be easily attainable. It is the fancied wants of the few, the selfishness of the few, that embitters the life of the world. Andrew Carnigie thinks himself a divinely ap- pointed sink into which wealth shall flow, he him- self to act as irrigator, turning the wealth in such direction as he thinks most desirable. If his work- men think different, straightway hordes of Huns, Poles, and Italians are imported to enable him to carry out his divinely appointed task. Eighty per cent. of the population of Chicago is foreign born, ninety per cent. of the population of New York is foreign born. I work now at the LARGEST wenn MILL IN THE STATES. Twice every day, that is at 8 a.m., and at 2 p.m., crowds of Turks, numbering from 50 to 200, stand in the road, in the gutter, toeing the footpath, and opposite the office door. They are marshalled into line by the day watchman, there to wait for the boss, on the mere chance that he may want a man, or two. When the boss has passed into the office, the Turks are driven away like hogs. lam not , exaggerating, reader. I can watch the little game ' any day. As a matter of fact it is so in every large I city in the States. Men who are paid to write "booming " articles for the press say nothing of this, and the mere tourist writer is never shown this dark side of the social question. The Turk and the Swede are remarkably well developed, and I may just here disabuse the English readers of something, which I, and they no doubt, have often read. You will never see in any of the States factor- ies the native-born American doing any hard work. He is educated to boss, and not to do hard work; he leaves that to the foreign-born, and generally ignorant, labourer. When you read again that the American works longer hours, and works harder, don't believe it. He is making your own flesh and blood do the work while he does the bossing. I have authority for saying this. Dr. Rainford in an article entitled "The rich and the poor" says—" The ordinary American may not take kindly to begging, I but be is certainly almost as unwilling to dig, (un- less it be for gold). He must have someone to dig for him,and so be first imported the Irishman,and he now, expressing a strong disinclination to digging, has taken to politics, and lets the Italian do the I work he used to perform." "The repugnance toi farm labour which seems to characterise the ' American is working havoc with the agricultural interests of this country. There are at present 30,000 able-bodied men in the city of Chicago who have neither employment nor any prospects of work." I have carefully noticed, gO far as it was possible for me to do so, in the works I am now engaged at, the native American boys engaged in any of the hard work, and I have not yet found one. I have been particular about these details so tar, because I , want what follows to be clearly understood. I am; going to make A FBARITTL CHARGE, and the two quotations I have made above may make what lam going to say somewhat hazy. The 30,000 idle Americans may, or may not be native- born. I have no means of proving it, or otherwise, but this I say, the native-born American who can say his grandparents were also native-born, is fast becoming a very scarce article. I have made, inquiries in the village in which I now reside, and I cannot bear of an American family of five child- ,en. In the California works at which I was previ- ously employed, myself, another Englishman, and an Irishman, had as many children as all the rest of the men put together, and there was a good num- ber. When Americans marry, they determine to have no children. The newspapers advertise mechanical and chemical preventives, and where these fail, the Dr. steps in and procures abortion. Now, why have I introduced this unsavory subject? Simply because it is so nearly allied to" the strug- gle for existence " question. Those who run may read. First, there is the American educational ' system labouring with the dead weight of ignorant European emigration at its heels. Second, there is the refusal of the cultured Americans to marry and have children, thus leaving evolution to work up as it may on its lowest grades. We therefore see tin intense and never-relaxing anxiety to be first in the struggle for existence, coupled with a horrid uni- versal blot on the escutcheon of America's domestic I life. I look amongst the "To lets " in the paper, , as I want a house ; every landlord, almost to a man insolently states that he wants no families of children. I go house hunting, and the first question , is," Have you any children ?" If I say yes, up goes the rent, or I am refused the house. Indeed the houses are not built for large families. To-day I have taken a house. It has two bedrooms and I have to pay 14s. a week rent, and my wages amount to 6s. Bd. per day. America is a great country, and don't forget it In the wire mills here there has JUST BEEN A STRIKE because the men would not learn the women how

to set the dies. About sixty men and twenty women came out. Of the latter only one or two wished to learn how to set the dies; the remainder were content with being mere wire pullers, and sympathised with the men. These women are all Finlanders and Irish (I may say here the Turks never bring their women folk to America) who have taken up the American idea not to marry, preferring not to marry, but, by reason of some accident or other, having now and again to perform maternal duties. The strike lasted a week, when the boss gave in, and the men and women returned to their wire drawing. I think the above is a terrible tale, if read between the lines. If readers would think what a great deal I could say, that I dare not say, they would be thankful that England is not 'America. But, I ask, are Englishmen doing their best to prevent England from becoming an imita- tion of America ? I ask Warringtonians to care- fully read Mr. Gladstone's article in the " Weekly Star" of Feb. sth on" The Labour Question." I ask them also to read the report as it appears of the Labour Commission, and then judge calmly whether a supporter of the Lord of Hatfield or a supporter of Mr. Gladstone is most likely to advance the greatest of all British interests, which is the right of the British workman to the soil and pro- ducts of his country. Greendale, March 17th, 1892.

BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blount," stxc., Jae. CHAPTER XXX. TUE SHIFTING SANDS. Bell Widdrington was sitting just outside of the cottage door in the cold clear spring sunshine, mending nets for Cuddy. She made a charming picture, with the light playing around her hair, bringing out its tints of gold and red, and the pure colour of her neck, as contrasted with the ribh peachy bloom of her cheek where the sun had caught it. Leaning against the doorway opposite to her stood Mr. Edward Wynne, his face puckered into a mass of wrinkles, with the effort required to rethin the gold-rimmed eyeglass, through which he sur- veyed the newly discovered divinity at whose shrine he worshipped_ He was becoming a laughing stock to the neighbourhood, by reason of his sudden infatuation of Bell. He dogged her footsteps when- ever she gave him the opportunity • and made him- self such a nuisance that the head of the family, dour-headed Cuddy, would fain have given him a. ducking to cool the ardour of his flame, had not Bell interposed to protect and save. Her interposition was a matter of surprise to the elder brother, who had never before perceived in her any tendency to flirtation or light behaviour. But in this case the girl merely laughed at his dis- pleasure, and still more at the warning with which he ended his brief jobation. Surely she was big enough and strong enough to take care of herself, she asked him mockingly. " Mebbe ay, and mebbe no, but he wasn't going to have folks clashing about anybody that was akin to him." However, looking at her strong, well-developed arms, and contrasting her with the puny figure of the little mannikin, who aspired to her favour, Cuddy felt satisfied ln his own mind that she was physically more than a match for Mr. Edward, and with an expressive grunt, in which was embodied a pious protest against the frivolity of young faces in general, that careful brother left her to her own devices. Bell had heard' nothing of Dick since the night when he left her side, with so many protestations of love and fidelity, two months previously. He had disappeared from the neighbourhood altogether, without a word or a sign to the woman who had been foolish enough to let him see what a hold he had upon her heart. • There were times when the knowledge of this preyed upon her mind, and at such times she was glad enough of any distraction that might servo to drive it away. How was she to be sure that he was true to het? He had already shown her that he valued his own liberty to do what she disapproved of more , highly than the prospect of a happy married life ' with her. Perhaps there were other reasons—how could she tell? One thing she did know. She was eery miserable, and occasionally very reckless. She laughed and sang incessantly; but there was a hard ring in her laugh, and a tremor in her song, unknown before. leddy thought she was simply perfection, though he wished she would not laugh at him and his this speeches so frequently. "Why, oh, why am I not a painter, to do justice to such charms ?" he poanred sentimentally, as for the twentieth time his eyeglass fell from its piece, and the beautiful vision grew blurred and indis- tinct. "Wonder if I could aver learn to do that? he asked aloud; "Your fingers move in and out of the meshes in a manner incomprehensible to me. it looks like a juggler's trick or a puzzle !" "Cuddy would mebbe be ill pleased if ye spoilt his net, or aw'd let ye hey a try, Mr. Wynne! Be thankful ye got o without any o' th' nasty jobs us fisher folks heel How wad ye like to bait the lines, for a change?" Teddy looked dawn at the heterogeneous mass of lines, hooka, and raw mussels lying coiled in a bas- ket at her feet and shuddered. Then he mastered his disgust manfully, and put on a languishing air. " Even that I could do for—for the sake of your approval, you beautiful sea-nymph !" Bell laughed. "Eh toe! it's not for me te mind one way or 'tether, its ruddy that's gestin' the say aboot the wark. There's some that's born te labour, an' some wi' silver spyunee thor mooths, Mr. Wynne !" " I would I'd been born a fisher lad for your sake, Bell !" " Hoots, man! Ye wish nowt o' th' kind," was Bell's impatient reply. Teddy knew that after such a snub as this it would be useless to pursue the subject To do him justice the little man was not half such a rake as he liked to bethought. It was fashionable to affect

vice. He meant no harm to the girl. For the flrat time in his life he was honestly in love, and with such a love no impure wish eould exist. "How plainly one hears the water running over the sand,' he remarked, after a pause, and Bell was devoutly thankful for a change of topic. "Ay, ower Plain at times for ma fancy. It's a sweet sound, but aw clinna care for't, somehow." "Indeed ! And why not ?" " Thor's queer stories telled about the sands &on by, where Yarrop burn runs ower them te the sea." "Are they dangerous?" "Dangerous enough! There's shiftin sands all alive an' greedy for somethin' te swallow, an' there's holes where a body might slip into by accident, and Breamiali tolled me that he once lost a cow an' a never be caught sight on again. An sad man doon at calf, lang sync, when he was a lad, drivin them a short cut ower the sands. There they wor one minnut alive, and kickin, an' down they sank afore his vary eyes, an' him stannin' not more than six feet off, neither able to help nor to hinder." "Dear me, that was strange! a heavy loss, too, for a poor man." "But poor Kitty Aynsley—her that lived here afore us—she had th' warst on it. Are a lone widow woman forbye, sore failed through trouble and the pains (rheumatism), that looked like a body of seventy, when she was full twenty years to the good. When she lost her lasses, she lost her all; I for they were upgrown and beginnin' to wark for he. an' to comfort hew-in her age. This was the way on't. The three on them had promised to gen 1 ower the burn to Farmer Bell's, away northward there, where a bit of a frolic was on; a kern supper aw fancy it might ha' been. The sharpest way to. th' farm lay along the sandhills, an' you bridge ye see up the water wasn't builded then; so Marget, her that was the eldest lass, an' the biggest and strongest of the two, Went doon afore the others, to make ready the boat to row them across. The burn was in flood, for it had been a deal o' rain away in I the tar west. It was a foggy afternoon, an' every now an' again they couldn't see one another for th' mist. But the two behind waited at th' door for the sound o' Marget's voice. She had promised to give them a hail when she was ready. They could hear the wetter rushin' like mad doon belaw, and the waves batterin' an' thundorin' away on the bench, far oot, but never was the voice they were listenin' for borne back to them. "'Gan thee ways, hinny, an' see what's gettin' thee sister,' says the mid wife at last, an' sure enough Molly, the youngest lass, went down after Marget, the eldeet. She laughed an' waved her hand back to her mother, an' that was the last on her. Poor aad Kitty ! She waited and waited through the gatherin' darkness till the night came on, but she never set eyes on them two lassos more. The waves thundered an' the watter rushed, an' once, strainin' h* ears she thowt she heard a faint cry, like, but it might only ha' been a gull or a pectsweep (plover) ; but eh me, neither of her bonny lasses ever corned back to her, Efter that she went, clean daft, in' kept callin' one or t'other all day long and all night, till she fair pined away, and died i' six months. Ye see it wesn't as if she'd lost them naterally, and given them a mensoful funeral, sia' could talk ower their illnesses and deaths wi' the neebors ; but just for them to leave her side like that, and niver no more on them, not even their .d.ear dead bodies to cry ower; no wonder the poor mother went off her heid ! Aw've often thowt of her of a misty night, at the beck end o' the year; cause it wes fra' this very hoose they went oot awll I together that October afternoon; an' when the wind comes up the gully with a sudden sough, as it often it does durin' autumn, it used to startle me, like as if were them two poor drowned lasses cryin' oot for help, and nobody nigh to give it !" "That is a sad story, but such things do not often happen, thank Heaven !" said Teddy, lightly. He did not. care for sad stories, and should not have had patience to listen to this one, had the narrator been any other than Bell. But while she talked he had leave to watch her changing expression, and that alone made him tolerant. "A sad story—it is terrible !" was murmured in a low voioe near to him; and turning, he beheld his sister, Lady Callerley, with white face, and eyes big like those of a frightened child. " Goodness, child, where have you sprung from? Silvia did not answer.

"Those sands you speak of, 8011, are they near here ?" Bell nodded, though she seemed annoyed that her story should have been overheard. "Just below, at the mouth o' th' Yarrop. But there's been no acoidant since that, and folks are careful now about crossin' them. Besides we've getten the bridge yonder—such like as it is," answered the fisher girl rather oontemptously ; and indeed the bridge in question, a ricketty wooden structure, did not seem sufficiently strong to with- stand any of the sudden floods incident to streams such as the Yarrop. "To leave her side—no more of them—not even their dear dead bodies to cry over," repeated Silvia, absently, "Oh, how would one feel oneself n such a case, I wonder ?" Some strange, indefinable feeling, terror, pity, presentiment, which was it! seized upon Lady Callerley as she spoke. She shuddered from head to foot; and had not Teddy, with admirable promp- titude, pet out his hand and supported her, she would assuredly have fallen. Only a moment and it was gone. Then she laughed rather wildly. "You silly Bell! Why do you try to frighten one with such gloomy tales? Don't you know how I. felt when I first came here, as though I were to be left alone, alone, in a big, sad, dreary world, like that poor old mother you speak of. Never mind ! The sun shines, and the spring is coming, and Teddy is here. Come, my little brother; come, for I want you! Jack—cousin Jack, is waiting for us to go a fishing up the stream. Let us laugh and be happy while we may, and bask in the sunshine. Come.'

CHAPTER XXXI. W HUSBAND AND WIFE. Iqrf Lady Callerley was sitting before the long swing- ing mirror in her room. She had dismissed her maid, and was brushing her curls in a slow dreamy I fashion. The wax candles burning in the silver sconces diffused a soft subdued light around, and showed up her reflection in a very pleasing way. Even though there was no one there to admire, it gave her a glow of satisfaction to note that she was looking her prettiest. Her eyes sparkled and the dimples came out in her cheeks at the thought. The dressing robe of Indian muslin which she wore, with its frillings and flouncings of soft and costly lace, suited her youthful roundness, and, threw up the pearly tints of her skin to perfection. Leaning her face upon her hands, she bent for- ward to gaze more critically. By rights such a face as that ought to have been fortunate in love. A childish wonder at the perversity of fate, and a self pity following upon the wonder, occupied her mind. Suddenly,. glancing upward, the stern, grave visage of her husband met her gaze. The expression he wore seemed to her to reprove her apparent vanity and weakness. Above all small frivolities himself, she fancied— wrongly as it happened—that he despised her for her failure to attain like heights of superiority. Like a child detected in some small fault or dis- obedience, she hung her pretty head at once. But when he still kept silence, a rebellious spirit began to arise within her. If he had wanted a wife who would reflect his virtues why had he not left her alone? It was not her fault but her misfortune that his tastes were a continual reproof to her, and that whatever she did found no favour in his eyes. When she reached this conclusion, she glanced at him furtively, from under her downcast brows. He was standing with folded arms; still, silent, impassive. It was impossible for her to bear this lo,r. Like a frightened bird struggled the heart wit in her bosom. "I cannot bear your silent presence, Lancelot," she said, with petulance. "If I have made you angry with me why do you not say so at once; in place of standing there like a reproachful ghost, waiting to be challenged to deliver its message " Sir Lancelot sighed, and drew nearer to her, but still kept his oppressive silence. "Lancelot, speak Are you angry with me?" "Angry with you, child? No. What right have Ito be angry with you ?" he said at last, • I am restless and miserable—that is all,"

His voice was low and tremulous with deep feel- ing, but Silvia mistook his meaning. It was his love for her and the apparent hopelessness of it to which he alluded, while she fancied it to be the family skeleton. Since Lady Callerley had made up her mind to be merry and to forget everything sad, to live in the present, cutting off the past; and shutting her eyes to the future—this persistent recurrence of a sad theme strangely irritated her. "Well, you are not the only one in the world who is miserable, I suppose t." she replied, lightly, and with studied indifference, "We all have our turns of that sort of thing; but for my part I have come to the conclusion that it is host never to think. There are generally some rays of sunshine which penetrate every cloud, and it is well to-bask in them while one can, and to forget the coldness of the shadow." . Sir Lancelot winced both at the tone and the I words. They sounded heartless and =feeling in the extreme. As she spoke of the rays of sunshine he recalled a scene he had come upon a.ecidentally that evening, and which had left a burning sonic of pain and injury rankling(' within him, a scene so apparently simple and natural that it was impossible for him to recent it openly. As he rode homeward through a deeply sunk lane he heard a sound of laughter; and looking around, discovered his wife, her brother, and young Breamish amusing themself mightily. Jack had climbed a bank to pick some branches of flowering may, and was trying the effect of them amongst Lady ()eller- ley's russet curls ; while Teddy was acting as critic, and pronouncing an opinion with the gravity of Sir Oracle. When the baronet chanced upon the scene the mirth and laughter died out suddenly, and they crave nod silent at 011 M The husband was a kill-j 'oy and a wet blanket; for whom no smiles beamed no words of gay greet- were forthcoming. He felt acutely commons of this fact, and it exasperated and maddened him. Was the innocent girl he had married developing into a heartless coquette? "What casts this hateful shadow in whictiiiyon are obliged to walk, Silvia ?" he asked, gloomily, "Is it the distasteful companionship of your husband ?" "I have had so much of that, truly," answered Silvia, with sudden scorn. 1 Sir Lancelot began to pace up and down the room ! impatiently. Pride, anger, jealousy, passion, were all striving together within him, and at any moment the impending storm might break forth, and sweep away all the barriers of self restraint he had erected so carefully. - Every now and again a few agitated words broke from him. "You are hard,—you are cruel, Silvia,—you will neither forget nor forgive! See me now—do I hot suffer—have I not yet endured enough to content you. I may not approach too near you—may not kiss you even. No. You shudder away from my , Caresses, and loathe the giver of them. So be it. But there is no need for you to fear me, child. You do not understand—that is what drives, me wild. DO poll think I care to have your body without your soul?" His face was convulsed and distorted by the emotion that tont him, and great beads of perspira- tion were on his brow. Silvia gave one glance at it, and immediately buried her own in her hands. Was it fear, or was it some other emotion that seemed to take possession of her, shake her whole being, and render her powerless and silent? - net- husband stopped before her suddenly. div.head: HOW MEN PROPOSE.
div.p: HOW MEN PROPOSE.

Some ladies at a five o'clock tea table have been comparing notes on the question of "how men pro- pose," and what light their experience has been able to throw en this subject has been reserved for the enlightenment of the readers of " Woman." No mention seems to have been made of the practice of going down on one, or sometimes on two knees but that has long been known to be only an obstin- ate conventionality of the stage. Generally, the admirers of these ladies seem to have had an un- happy propensity to propose at the wrong time or in the wrong place. But the most interesting pro- posal reported by one of their number was that of an absent-minded young man who used notes. The young lady was giving a little reception, and, of course, her time was much occupied. The young man perceived that this would be the case, and, to facilitate matters, he brought with him a memo- randum. "I afterwards," says the object of his ill-starred devotion, "found it on the floor, where he had dropped it in his agitation." It was:" Men- tion rise in salary. Mention loneliness. Mention pleasure in her society. Mention prospects from Uncle Jim. Never loved before. Propose."

div.head: BRAVE POLICEMAN.
div.p: A BRAVE POLICEMAN.

Police Constable Joseph Sparrow, of Pontefract, has received a gratuity of £2O, besides a handsome compliment from Mr. Justice Wright at the West Riding Assizes. Few persons would perhaps care to win these rewards in the same fashion. Sparrow was walking on a lonely part of the railway late one night, or rather early one morning, when lie overtook two suspicious men, and asked them what theywere doing there at that hour. They replied by throwing stones at him, cutting his mouth and eye and loosening three of his teeth. He closed with one of them, and while they were struggling he noticed that a train was approaching; then they rolled into the other rails, and he had mastered his man,when the other ruffian came up and hit him on the head several times. They then tried to take his staff from him, and failing in this they knocked his head on the rails, and one kicked him on the back of the head. One of his assailants then sug- gested that they should throw him under the train, but luckily another constable arrived to his assist- ance, and both the men were captured. The two ruffians, who have been proved to have attempted to commit a burglary that night, have been sen- tenced each to seven years' penal servitude.

div.head: APPEALING TO ;THEIR VANITY.
div.p: APPEALING TO ;THEIR VANITY.

During the early excesses of the French Revolu- tion a rabble of men and women were rioting in the streets of Paris. Lafayette appeared and ordered a young artillery officer to open fire upon them with two cannon. The officer begged the general to let him try first to persuade them to withdraw. "It is useless to appeal to their reason," said the general. " Certabily," answered the officer; "and it is not to their reason, but to their vanity I would appeal." The officer rode up to the front of the mob, doffed his cocked hat, pointed to the guns and said, "Gen- tlemen. will have the kindness to retire ; for I am ordered to shoot down the rabble." The street was cleared at once; for none could brook the idea of being classed with the scum of the city. During the agrarian riots which disturbed England in 1832 a mob of rick-burners and machine-breakers appeared at the old mansion of two elderly maiden ladies. The walls of the hall were decorated with suits of armour and, antique weapons—pikes, hal- berds, swords, and battle-axes. The mob clamoured for the weapons and for drink. The ladies refused their demands, and when the mob seemed ready to resort to violence, Miss Bctty, the elder of the ladies went up to the leader, a hideous-looking man, and said: " You, too, of all the people in the world! I'm not surprised at these poor misguided creatures, But that such a good-looking, intelligent man as you should attack two defenceless women does astonish me. It ou are the man I should have looked to for protection. But you are not the man I took you for. Never again will I trust to good looks." There was no standing up against that complaint, The man took off his hat, and said, "Come, old lady, we aint so bad its all that, only give us some beer. We would not harm a hair of your head." "No, I know that;' retorted Miss Betty. " You can't; I wear a wig." 'the moo roared with laughter, and retired without another word.

div.head: MASTER OF MI OCCASION.
div.p: MASTER OF MI OCCASION.

-- General Gordon was a man who knew how to use the decisive moment, and resort, if necessary, to the most extreme measures in order to insure a neces- sary success. When he was sent to aid in putting down the Tai-ping rebellion in China, he found the array of defence to be a curious body of soldiers. Every available man had been pressed into the ser- vice, sailors without a ship, deserters from the enemy, gaolbirds, pirates, outlaws, roughs, and tramps of all nations and characters. This was the self-christened " Ever-victorious Army." When Gor- don assumed the command, he declared that there should be no more sacking and burning of towns, and when, against his orders, a city had been plun- dered, he removed the officer who had condoned the offence, and replaced him by a better man. At this the troops rebelled. They held a meeting, the resnit of which was a round robin, stating that unless their wishes were consulted there would be trouble. And there was trouble, but not in the direction they had indicated. The new commander in his turn called a meeting, and the discontented leaders, growling and swearing, assembled in the barrack yard. "Now," said Gordon, appearing suddenly, " fall in!" They refused. From that moment they began to understand him. Quiet and unassuming as he had been, in an instant he rose before them the embodi- ment of passion and unconquerable will. "The name of the ringleader! Quick ! ' he cried. " Out with it, or within an hour one man in every five of you shall be sh at !" This was received with a loud and savage groan. One ruffian in the crowd groaned a little louder than his fellows, and quick as a flash of lightning Gordon had him dragged from the ranks, and ordered him to be shot. Within an hour the rest of the valiant mutineers were on their knees, tendering their submission and roaring for mercy. In the fifteen following months he had broken up the rebellion, saved millions of money, and preserved countless men and women from tor- ture and death. He had actually saved a mighty empire and a throne, and, more than that, he had won the love and absolute trust of his extraordin- ary at my. THE BOLTON OUTRA.6IE. -144 At Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, Lord' Chier ustice Coleridge passed sentence of 12 years' penal servitude on James Whitley, a labourer, aged 32, who on the 18th February last, in a secluded street in Bolton. cut the throat of a married woman named Elizabeth Mather, with whom he had cohabited for three or four years. The woman's life was in danger for some weeks, and she is still so feeble that during the trial of her assailant on Saturday she, fainted, and had to be carried out of court.. asiusmion

apparent on visiting the destructors, and the sulphurous fumes, dust, Etc., which escaped from the lires when the doors at the front of the furnaces were opened, rendered the platform over the furnaces and buildings generally simply unbearable, and dangerous to health. Much of this nuisance might be avoided by more thorough venti- lation of the roof, and I would also suggest more efficient lighting. The platform ' was too much covered with refuse which did not seem deposited sufficiently near the cell openings, and, further, the incombustible mate- rial, such as tins, rots, Sec., formed an unusually large accumulation for this part of the works. A point for the Corporation to decide is whether the cells are not overworked, and, perhaps, insufficient for coping satis- factorily with the refuse of an increasing town. Al- though I did not recognise any odour from the chimney, I can well understand that a nuisance from this cause may arise in the district of the Rural Sani- tary Authority, varying with the state of the at- mosphere and direction of the wind, say at a dis- tance of 150 to 500 yards from the works, and I would recommend the introduction of a secondary furnace, or cremator, for more completely consuming the products of combustion. If the Corporation provided such an apparatus it is possible that the gases escaping from the somewhat low chimney would be rendered inodorous and free from objection on the part of the residents of the neighbourhood. Before concluding my remarks, 1 must say that, on the whole, the mode of collecting the refuse of Warrington seems to be an admirable one, and the treatment is carried out with great efficiency. The above suggestions, I believe, would further improve the character of the works, and, it is hoped, remove any reasonable cause for complaint. Thanks are due to the two members of the Sanitary Committee, to Dr. Gornall, and other officials, who so courteously gave every Infor- mation to Dr. Sephton and myself respecting the methods adopted for dealing with the town's refuse." Alderman Burgess added that he did not propose to make any sug- gestion upon the report. Dr. Sephton would report upon the matter to the Rural Sanitary Authority, and in the meantime it would not be wise for him (Alderman Burgess) to comment upon it. He might say, however, that on the day of the visit to Longford Depot, Dr. Seph- ton and Dr. Sergeant visited the depots in Lythgoes-lane. Dr. Sephton remarked "In very good condition," and Dr. Sergeant" Very well worked.' He (Alderman Bur- gess) thought that was satisfactory. The alder- man then dealt at considerable length with the estimates of the Committee. In conclusion he said that as that was probably the last time he would stand in that room making an explanation about the estimates for the Sanitary Committee or any other committee, he wished them to look at the position they were in as a Corporation. He had been a menabereif the Corporation for many years. Councillor Dixon : You have, and no one knows that better than we do, to our sorrow. (Interruption, and cries of " Order.") Alderman BURGESS, continuing, said that Alderman Holmes and himself were put down as having been 35 years members of the Council, and he wished the mem- bers to look at the position they were in. He would refer to the rates which had been laid since 1857. During the first ten years the rates amounted to ss. 10d. in the £, the next ten years to ss. 10d., during the next ten years there was a declension, to 53.81 d., and the last five years gave them a reduction to ss. 13.1. That was a satisfac- tory declension. considering the work that had been done. He had shown that there had been a declension in the Warrington rates, and he would mention a few items to show what had been done in the way of expenditure, although the rates had gone down since 1872. They had called into existence a Town Hall, and Bridge-at, had been widened. Then there was the expenditure connected with the School Attendance Committee and the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital, an extra museum and library rate, £350 for a medical officer of health, and public analyst £lOO, recreation ground at Howley £35 a year, market ess„ten- Rion, public sewers, and the price of gas had been twice reduced. Had these and other expenses not been in- curred, the rates would have been a shilling in the £ less. Councillor MUIR drew the attention of the Council to the fact that the Chairman of the Sanitary Corn- mittee had intimated that in the estimates there was provision for an increased cost for pails. With regard to the removal of the pails, he wished to give expression to a complaint that on account of the tremendous noise which the men made in that operation, it was impossible to obtain any sleep after six o'clock of a morning. (Laughter.) The men engaged in their removal also knocked the pails about, as if it 'cost. the Corporation nothing at all to repair them. Councillor F. A. 120132111T8 said that according to the estimates, there was a prospect of having an extra ex- penditure of about 20 per cent. The extra expenditure on Longford depot would amount to something like £7OO. Ever since he had become a member of the Coun- cil, when the estimates were presented, it was al- ways stated that some expenditure was extraordinary. It was always asserted that if the expenditure was al- lowed they would be amply rewarded by results. Alderman BURGESS: So you have been. (Laughter.) Councillor F. A. ROBERTS begged to differ with the worthy Alderman in regard to his assertion. The cost of maintaining the Longford Depot was £3,327, and the price realized for the sale of the excreta was £2,250, showing a loss of £l,OOO per annum. They had always been led to believe that the Longford Depot would be a source of profit. Alderman Buroatss :At is now. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS,: No, no ! The estimates show a loss of £l,ooo.—He did not wish to criticize the work of the Sanitary Committee—to criticize the statements which they made, and which were calculated to delude the Corporation into the belief that the works were not being worked at a loss, when they were really being worked at a loss. If the committee would only come to the Council, and say in effectthat the system which they had for dealing with excreta was the best they could get, and that the loss caused in its use was so much, the Cor- poration would know where they were. He had hoped and believed up to the present point that the Longford process was the best means they could get to deal with the excreta, and he had been confirmed in that belief by the glowing statements which had been made from time to time. But instead of the Longford Depot improving, he found that it was going worse. He thought that it was about time the Corporation set themselves to consider if the evaporation principle was the best to deal with the excreta of the town. He gave the Alderman every credit for his industry, but he thought in all seriousness that the matter should be considered. He was by no means as sanguine of, the prospect which lay be- fore Longford, as he was two or three years ago. He asked if Alderman Burgess could tell the Council how many towns from which deputations had been sent to view the Longford works had adopted the Warrington plan of dealing with excreta ? (Hear, hear.) He had never heard of any town adopting the system in vogue in War- rington, and there had teen numerous deputations to visit the works. If the plan adopted by Warrington had been a good one, he was sure that some towns would have followed it. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that as he had to leave the meeting early, he would like to express his surprise and sincere regret that Alderman Burgess had decided not to appear again as the chairman of the Sanitary Commit- tee. He felt sore that he would only be expressing the opinion of every member of the Corporation, and of each person outside of the Corporation, when he said that the resignation of the Alderman would be viewed with sin- cere regret. (Hear, hear.) Continuing, he said that he was one of the members of the Sanitary Committee who had never believed it possible to work the Longford de- pot at a profit. He thought that there had been a great deal of misunderstanding in regard to assertions which had beea made. They were capable of explanation. What he did contend for was that,as far as they knew at present, it was an utter impossibility to treat excreta, conveyed to Longford and also ashes, in such a manner as to result in a profit to the ratepayers. It was no use making statements which could not be verified. Figures were awkward things to deal with. It seemed to him, on the face of the figures which had been submitted, that there was a loss. There was a difference between the amount of money received for the manufactured article and the cost of producing it of about £l,OOO a year. He was prepared to take those figures, but he would state unhesitatingly that to dispose of the vast amount of filth which was created, including about 20,000 tons of cinders and rubbish, for £l,OOO, was a cheap bargain, and a cheaper one he did not think they would be likely to get. It was the duty of the Corpora- tion to reduce the difference between the cost of pro- duction and the inziome from the manufactured article to:the lowest possible point consistent with the proper management of the institution. (Hear, hear.) Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGZ said that, to his mind, the accounts were misleading. There was a constantly growing population, and the expenses of the Sanitary Committee must necessarily increase. Instead of a lump sum being fixed, he suggested that an amount be stated In relation to each head of population. Councillor Duos strongly criticized what he consi- dered to be the defective machinery at Longford. Councillor BEAMAN said that Dr. Sergeant had told him only two weeks ago that Warrington had the clean- liest way of dealing with excreta of any works that he had ever visited. He would hazard the prediction that Longford in the immediate future would become a pay- ing concern. Councillor BIitiTHURST stated that he noticed in the estimate for horse labour, 4,000 days at Bs. ed. per day, and another item of 2,200 days at Bs. 6d., which made a total of £2,635. He believed that the Paving and Sewerage Committee had a contract for having the labour supplied at 6s. 6d. Although he did not think that amount was sufficient recompense, yet he thought that if the cominittee were to give an increased amount, it would pay them to let out the contract. He was con- fident that a large saving could be effected. He also advised the Committee to.give Mr. Diggle's plan a fair trial. Councillor PLIIMPTON 'stilea that he had listened to the statements which had bedn Made in regard to the Long- ford Depot. The Chairman of the Sanitary Committee had asserted that it was a paying concern. Councillor Roberts said that it never would pay, and another mem- ber had said that it would. He thought that these gentlemen were in a bit of a muddle and the ratepayers should know exactly how matters stored. In the accounts there was an amount of £6OO for sundries. He would like to have seen an amendment proriosed,but he hardly liked to take upon himself the responsibility of composing one, when there was evidently no one likely to support it. Alderman DiTEGESS in replying said that very many of the deputations which came to Warrington were merely out for a holiday. He did not wish to say thing disres- pectful. Counciller FIEATON Are we to understand that that is what you do? (Laughter.) Alderman BURGESS: Oh ! no. The speaker then asked Councillor F. A. Roberts had made some mention about that being the last occasion on which he (Alderman Burgess) would have an opportu- nity of laying before the Council a proposal like the present one. They could hardly expect much otherwise. He had never spoken of resignation. It was not in him. He would never dream of such a thing. The period for which he was elected expired at the end of the year, and it was not unreasonable to suppose that he would be set at liberty. He had spent a great deal of pleasant time with the Council. Few people had had such little con- tention as he had. He had fully enjoyed himself. (Laughter.) That night had been an exceedingly pleas-: ant one to him. It was somewhat disappointing to find when he asked for an increase of expenditure that no one had the courage to move an amendment. (Laughter) He was still, as he had always been, onbeaten. (Voices: "Ohl Oh !") This disappointment caused a gloom to i be thrown over the meeting. (Hear, hear.) • DEATH OF MEL, BEADEL, M.P.no I 141,1 Mr. Wm. James Beadel, the member for the Mid or Chelmsford Division of Essex, died on Tuesday after- noon, at his residence, Hutton Hall, Brentwood, Essex. The hon. member, who had been seriously ill for some time, was born at Witham, Essex, in 1828 ; was a well- known estate agent and surveyor, and was president of the Surveyors' Institution, and also a magistrate and deputy-lieutenant for his native county. He was a Conservative, and was first elected to Parliament for the same division in 1885.
-•-- MOCKING TRAGEDY IN
BELFAST,

--- MURDER OF A WIFE AND TWO CHILDREN. An awful tragedy, took place in Belfast, on Wednesday morning, a woman and her two little children being brutally murdered. It appears that at a quarter to 11 o'clock a gunsmith named Allan Spiller, who has been out of employment owing to ill-health for the past seven I months, met Constable Kennedy on the Antrim-road, close to the police harracks, and quietly informed him that he had murdered his wife and family in the attic of the house No 24, Hillman-st. His hands were covered with blood, and the Constable, believing that some- thing terrible had happened, brought the self-accused murderer to the police barracks close at hand. , A number of men went to the house indicated, and on obtaining admission they proceeded to the attic alluded to by Spiller, where one of the most appalling sights ever witnessed in Belfast met their gaze. Lying on a mat- tress in the centre of the floor, another mattress being thrown over them, were the bodies of Sp!ller's wife and her two children, Jim, aged three, and Nellie, aged two, all with their throats,cut from ear to ear, and quite dead., The gash in the woman's throat extended almost from the back of the neck to the front of the throat, and was fully two inches in width. Her head had evidently been battered in with a hammer after the razor, with which the deed was committed, had been brought into requisi- tion. From the abrasions on the woman's left hand and from other marks on the body it was quite evident that a fearful struggle for life had taken place. On each side tof the poor creature lay her two little children, each with its throat cut, the heads being almost severed from the bodies. On ascertaining that the victims of the triple tragedy were beyond medical aid, Sergeant M'Aleese, after leaving two constables in charge of the house, hastened to the police barracks and izformed District- . •spector M'Ardle, who thereupon had Spiller removed to toe central Police Station, where a formal charge of murder in each case was entered against him, and pris- oner was remanded.

AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS BILL.—On the motion to go ' into Committee on the Agricultural Holdings Bill, Mr. Cobb moved an Instruction empowering the Committee to insert clauses in the Bill, creating popularly elected parish councils, with initiatory powers of acquiring and letting land. After an unexpectedly brief debate, in the course of which Mr. Chaplin opposed the proposed Instruction, the House divided, 161 voting with Mr. Cobb, 178 against. The narrow majority of 27 was loudly cheered by the Opposition.—Mr. Stephens next moved an instruction empowering urban sanitary authorities or vestries to exercise powers of acquiring, selling, letting, and managing land under the Bill by voluntary arrangement with the owners, subject to approval by the County Council.—Mr. GLADSTONII brief speech, supported the proposal, arguing that it is well to accept half a loaf when the alternative is to re- main without bread. The Liberal party, Mr. Gladstone said, held it to be of vital importance to the Bill that there should be established essentially local bodies pos- sessed of local information to deal with the proposals of the Bill.—Mr. CHAPLIN could not accept the instruction, and on a division it was rejected by 174 votes against 151. Sir William Floimnswoitra said the Assessment Committees were complaining that they had no guidance, and it was to give hem that as nearly as possible that the present bill was trought in.—Sir HENRY Jpodas said the burden upon manufacturers should be equal in different localities, and the second reading of the bill would mean that something must be done to render the law definite and clear.—Mr. RITCHIE said the Government saw no reason to depart from the neutral attitude they had hitherto adopted in this matter, but, speaking for himself, he gave a cordial support to the motion. He thought the fears of the agricultural interest were greatly exaggerated. In voting for the second reading he was supporting a measure for more clearly defining the law, and when the bill got into Committee the Government would have to see that its provisioas did not go beyond the lines on which it was supposed to rest. On a division, the second reading was carried by 232 to 122. The Gaming Act (1845) Amendment Bill passed through Committee, and on the motion of Mr. FOWLBE was read the third time.

The House adjourned at ten minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four. MISCHLLANEOUS.—The Pilotage Provisional Order Bill and the Local Government (Ireland) Provisional Order (No. 1) Bill were read a second time. The Bills of Sale and the Public Authorities Protection Bill passed through their Committee stage without amendment. On the motion of the Lord Chancellor, Lord Thring was added to the Select Committee on the Statute Law Revision Bill. The House adjourned at fifteen minutes to five, until Monday the 2nd of May.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Trmasner. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS.-Mr. Mai-maws, answering a question, said extra police had been drafted into Durham from Lancashire and Yorkshire at the instance of the Chief Constable. The Attorney General, in reply to Mr. Legh, said the views of Nonconformists on the subject of the attendance of registrars at marriages were so conflicting that he doubted if it would be possibls to deal with the subject until they had had a Parliamentary inquiry. The Attorney General informed Mr. P. O'Brien that Deeming could only be brought to England and tried far other offences in the event of the proceedings at present pend- in Australia resulting in his being discharged. THE RAILWAY BREACH OF PRIVILEGE.

On the order for the attendance of of Mr. J. W. MACLURE in his place and for the appearance of Mr. J. F. Buckley, Mr. W. B. Hawkins, and Mr. J. Conacher at the bar of the House, the Speaker stated the findings of the Select Committee on the flours of Railway Servants as to the action taken by those four gentlemen in re- gard to John Hood, late stationmaster on the Cambrian Railways, and called upon them for any statement they ' might wish to make. Mr. MACLIIRIC first and the other gentlemen afterwards apologised for any infringement of the rules or privileges of the House which they might have committed. sir Michael Hicks- Beach thought that Mrs. MacClure and his colleagues had made the most ample apology, and that the neces- sities of the case would be met by a resolution, which he moved, declaring that these gentlemen had committed a breach of privelege and that they should be admon- ished by Mr. Speaker. Mr. T. P. O'Connor moved to add an amendment calling upon the Company to reinstate Hood or to compensate him. Mr. 'P. P. O'Connor's amendment was rejected by 274 to 159. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach's resolution was carried by 340 to 70.

div.head: RAINHILL MURDERS.
div.p: THE RAINHILL MURDERS.
CROWDS OF VISITORS TO THE VILLSGE

On Sesslay ,and Saturday afternoon the villiage of Rainhill was the rendezirOdi.of crOivde6rtpeetators, exceeding those of any one day since the place became notorious through the nefarious misdeeds of Deeming. ,On Saturday the main road to Warrington was tinder a • perpetual cloud of dust, caused by the cycles and car- riages which in incessant strings, sometimes three' and four abreast, came rushing up from Liverpool and other places. On Sunday the place was taken by storm; ['special 'busses were run from Warrington and St. Helens and neighbouring towns, while the arrive-10,y train I were simply without number. Special officials .were put on duty to cope with the traffic, which was probably the , heaviest .Rainhill has seen since it became a station. The ' road from the village up to Lawton-read wag for about two hours almost impassable ; and as for Lawton-road, it was packed as far as the villa, and beyond till it could , not possibly accommodate any more sightseers. There was a long, patient, but good-natured struggle to get in front of the villa, but many of the thousands who came from a distance—some of them, it was said, having journeyed thirty or forty miles—had to return home dis- appointed, being unequal to the effort of elbowing their way to the front. The hedges and trees in the vicinity Were put under requisition, and everything ,the curious people could lay their hands on in near con- tact with the villa and grounds was taken away. I Even had anyone got inside, there was nothing but the ' wreck of the former tenant to be seen. The flags of the kitchen have been removed, the corner cupboard is gone, the doors have disappeared, and the pit which formed the graves of the victims have been filled up and made level. lathe course of their operations, Madame Tus- saud's workmen have not come upon any further criminal indications. An attempt, it is understood, has been made to get the villa for exhibition purposes,but it is believed that the terms on which the land is held prevents this, even if otherwise there were any intention of entertain- ing such a proposition. It is stated in the village that arrangements are being made for a monstre excursion to Rainhill from a distance about Easter. Meanwhile, the sleepy villagers are shaking themselves together and putting themselves into shape for making a profit out of their notoriety. Hitherto only a few days have benefitted by Deeming's career in a pecuniary sense. On Sunday special efforts were made in the way of catering for the crowd, but it was necessarily on a small scale, and it was fortunate for the thousands who came trooping in that they brought some " provender "with them. Mr. Short's hetet was literally ransacked of everything eatable and drinkable. Monday was a woman's day at Rainhill, when the village was crowded ; but hardly a man was to be seen. J ladies, who came from far and near in waggonettes snd by rail, went over all the spots of interest in the tragedy, and carried off from the grave of the victims most of the wreaths, which they were "requested not to touch." The day was very fine and the crowd evidently enjoyed the outing much. The hostelry of Mr. Short was much run upon, and the hat of Deeming was fitted on many a fair head. A party of distinguished female visitors could not be satisfied until they had seen the bed- room at the Commercial which Deeming occupied during ' his stay there. The kitchen where he took his meals was also looked at with awe, and the trinkets he gave to Miss Barry, the barmaid, were surveyed with great curiosity. The shop of Mrs. Mather was also besieged by the fair sex, and many articles purchased as mementoes. THE PRISONER PHOTOGRAPHED. HOW HE GOT RID OF.HIS MOUSTACHE. MELISOMINE, SIINDIY.—Three excellent photographs of the prisoner, one full face, and one from each side, have now been obtained. When he was again placed in posi- tion, Deeming rose and exclaimed " I won't be photo- graphed." The deputy governor, who was present, said " You will do what you are told. Sit down again at once." Seeing that he could gain nothing by disobeying Deeming then quietly submitted to the operation. He has since been very quiet. He is allowed to wear his own clothes, but is not supplied with any luxuries, though he now takes advantage of the privilege of having his meals sent in to him from a neighbouring restaurant. His food before it reaches him is carefully examined by the authorities. Deeming is stripped and searched every night before retiring to rest, and his every movement is watched through an iron grating in the door by the wardens stationed outside. He continues to ask at intervals for Miss Rounsevell, who absolutely refuses to go to the gaol for the purpose of according him an inter,- view. A telem am which has been received from Perth states that the cell where the accused was confined there has been examined, and from the appearance of the hairs of his moustache which have been found it is evident that about three-fourths of them, as formerly conjectured, were plucked nut by the roots and that that the remains.' der were broken off. This telegram proves that the story as to the prisoner being shaved by two policemem is a mere concoction. MELBOURNZ,SATUItDAY.-1 he detectives have been over. hauling the luggage of Wi 'Hams, alias Deeming,a/ias Swan- ston,and have made some discoveries of great importance at the present time. These include a marriage certificate, dated "Parish Church, Rainhill, September 22nd, 1891," a time table giving the arrivals and departures of the trains between Rainhill and Liverpool, a lot of Christmas cards which had been sent to Emily Mather from friends at Rainhill and Liverpool, her Bibles, prayer-books, and other devotional volumes, a number of ornaments, and articles of dress belonging to the unfortunate woman ,which have already been identified as having been worn by her during the voyage out on the Kaiser. More gruesome in character are a knife and a hammer-headed axe. the possession of which will tell strongly against the prisoner. They are of a kind used only in medical examinations, the knife being a dissecting knife. Both bear witness of usage. Mr. Marshall Lyle, the solicitor for the defence, had another long interview with the prisoner to-day. He appeared to be greatly amused at the statement that he had made a confession to Mr.Llaynes,hia Perth solicitor,of his connection with the last two " Jack the Ripper " murders. He laughs the matter to scorn. When ques- tioned by Mr. Lyle as to his whereabouts when the South African murders took place, of which Detective Brandt accuses him, were committed, he hesitated for a moment, and then said if he were ever charged with the Johannesburg crime he would easily be able to prove an alibi. Every precaution continues to be taken by the gaol authorities to prevent Williams committing suicide, and with this view they have finally refused to return him his spectacles. The governor of the prisoa has, however provided him with a remedy for his alleged shortsighted- ness, by having a powerful magnifier affixed to the table in his cell to enable him to read. For this atten- tion Williams professed to be very grateful. The Raiser Wilhelm steamer, in which Williams made the passage to Melbourne last year, has arrived at Ade- laide on her return voyage. One of the photograhs of the prisoner taken as Deeming was shown to the captain and officers, and they at once identified it as a likeness of Williams, whom they remembered as an outward- bound passenger in November. Far from endorsing Miss Mather's glowing account of his conduct on the voyage, they describe him as a ruffian and scoundrel of the lowest type. INQUEST AT MELBOURNE. PAINFUL REVELATIONS. Mimeouttee, TITASDAY.—The adjourned inquest on the body of Emily Mather, who was known as Mrs. Williams was opened this morning, at the City Court, which was. crowded to suffocation. By order of the Coroner, the,, prisoner Williams, alias Deeming, was brought into court, and was assigned a seat in front of the dock. The evidence previously taken was read over. It included the post-mortens examination, and testified to the woman having aied from violence, her skull having been bat- tered in and her throat cut. The owner of the house at Windsor. where the murder was committed, was the next witness. He described how prisoner, whom he identified in court, and whom he had known under the name of Drouin, took his house, on December 16, 1891, for a short term. Then he went on to narrate how on March 3, when he was showing a lady over the empty house he noticed a horrible odour, how on looking over the premises thoroughly he obeerved, that the hearthstone in one room seemed slightly higher than its proper level, and how he had the stone lifted.' Amid intense excitement witness spoke of the ghastly discovery of the doubled-up body of the deceased, and stated that he at once sent for the police. The sergeant of police, who had been called in by the previous witness, gave confirmatory evidence, stating that the body was encased in cement and lying in a shallow hole beneath the hearthstone. Evidence of identification was then given, several witnesses deposing to their having recognised the remains as those of Mrs. Williams, and also swearing that the prisoner in court was the Williams who passed as the husband of the de- ceased. Mr. Ilirschfeldt, who went to Perth to identify the prisoner, said he conversed with Deeming on board the Ballarat, and the accused said. " I don't know how any- one could hurt poor little Emily." He also remarked that if he were found guilty lie intended to write a his- tory of his life which would startle the world. . The wit- ness told him that he had compromised himself by Mat- ing off his moustache, and that he would certainly be hanged. Deeming listened to this evidence with in- terest, and laughed when Hirschfeldt mentioned th E like- lihood of his execution. Miss Kate Rounsevell, whom he was on the point of marrying when arrested, entered the court, recognised hft, and bowed' but he was not at all perturbed for he; salutation. During the adjourn- ment for luncheon lie walked into the courtyard, and was annoyed because he could not get a cigar. The evi- dencegiven in the afternoon dealt chiefly with his pur- chase of cement, the noises heard at the house at Wind- sor, and the prisoner's wanderings about the country under different aliases, but always with the canary and cage so frequently mentioned in the case. A matrimonial agent told how the accused, under the name of Duncan, sought another wife; and a witness who had been en- gaged to convey Deeming's luggage stated that he found a card bearing an invitation to the dinner at the Commercial Hotel, at Rainhill. The inquest Was ads iourned till Wednesday. '
