THE RESUMED INQUEST. STARTLING FRESH EVIDENCE.

MELBOURNE, W EDNESDAY. —The proceedings were opened at 10 o'clock this morning before Dr. Neifl, the deputy eel-oiler. The rush of the public, though heavy, was not nearly so great as expected. Girls from 16 tO. matrons of, any age wile seea, fighting, fumins.,, and faint- ing in the effort to get in, while behind them were a couple of thousand of the male sea struggling vigorously with the same object. The prisoner entered surrounded by policemen, the appearance of the man altogether being a startling sur- prise to those who had previously only known him by newspaper portrai ts. He is a most insignificant-100 ling short, spare, and stumpy, with ragged hairs covering his face and an incipient beard just beginning to grow on his shaven chin. He has sharp restless eyes,widc ' mouth, thin lips, and a perpetual somewhat irritating half sardonic smile. When the Coroner directed that the evidence previously taken should be read over, the ac- cused terned jokingly to his solicitor and passed some flippant remarks. Lonisa Atkinson, a widow, who earns her living by needlework, said in December last she was living near Andrew-st., Windsor, and on the 23rd and 24th of the month she heard words of anger at No. 57, indicative of quarrelling and apparently those of a man and woman. By the sound something had evidently been thrown. The witness deposed that she saw a woman half way up a lane at the side of -the house in great con fusion and agita- tion. Upon a photograph of Mrs. Williams being shown to the witness, she said that it resembled the woman to whom she referred. Charles James leCall, a clerk with Beauchamp and Porters, auctioneers, in Coilens-st.,testified that Williams came to him on January 4th, and had a talk concerning the sale of certain goods. He gave the name of Harry Dawson. He went to Williams's place, and the latter gave him a list of goods including a bucket, a pan, a spade, and a broom. -Dawson was identified with The bucket, pah, and broom were purchased at the sale by a man named Henry Wilmot. He was neat called and I identified the articles produced in court as the same. The 'pan had contained apparently only cement,and a quantity of cement walstill adheringto the sides. The spade was new, but one rorner of it had been bent as if it had been
_ gave him a list of goods including ' spade, and a broom.—Tfiiiiion
,lused-against a hard substance. W

had the broom, a hair broom' and also the bucket.-- Henry Inglis, a draper, testified to being present at the auction and buying a wicker chair, which was brought over by Williams on the Kaiser Wilhelm. Edward Vivian testified that in December he sold to Williams a chronograph watch for £7, which Williams left with him to be cleaned and regulated. He ordered it to be sent to Mr. Dobbin at the Criterion Hotel. It was forwarded there, but returned, though Williams after- wards called for it and took it away. On January 4 Williams bought of him an opera glass for £2, giving in payment a cheque on the bank of Australasia for that amount. The cheque was signed " A Dawson." He afterwards made other purchases, which he paid for by cheque under the same name. He bought a nap- kin ring, and ordered it to be engraved with the letters "B. S." and two rings, the whole bill being £25 or £3O. Witness took the goods to ‘Villiams's home, but Williams did not pay for them. He said his wife was ill from the influenza, at Sydney, and appeared much distressed. d A few days afterwards he received a letter as follows : "Dear old boy, I am leaving for Sydney. I have re- ceived a wire from Mrs. DAwson, who is very ill. I will send you a cheque. Address me at Albury House, Itcckdale, near Sydney." He never saw or heard from Williams after that, and after Williams had left his shop he missed two other rings. Richard Thomas Smith, an accountant, testified that he was introduced to:Williams under the name of Date-- son in December last. - Williams said that his uncle had died and left him an extensive property located next to Bennett's jewellery store in Cheapside, London. It was worth, be said, from £20,000 to £30,000. He went at Williams's request to a book shop where a sale was to take place. Williams said his wife was very fond of reading. Williams made several purchases at the sale, and said he was going to furnish a house. On the 9th of January he said he had received a letter to the effect that she was worse, and he was afraid he would have to go to Sydney. He saw Williams again on the 12th January, but not after that. He identified the prisoner as the man in question. Samuel Farrell, an accountant in the Bank of Austra- lia, testified that an account was opened with that bank by Harry Dawson, on the Bth of January, 1892. He did not know the person. Fifteen pounds were deposited. He produced two cheques and the signature book, the three signatures corresponding. On the Bth of January the deposit of 02 was made in the shape of a cheque- from M' Lean Brothers and'Rigg. This was a corrobora- tion of the previous testimony concerning the auction sale_ 1

div.head: • TRIAL OF DEEMING VERDICT OF WILFUL MURDER.
div.p: • TRIAL OF DEEMING VERDICT OF WILFUL MURDER.

MELBOURNE, TECURSDAY.—The coroner's inquest has found a verdict of wilful murder against Williams, alias Deeming. During the proceedings to-day, the prisoner disp!ayed the same effrontery and forced jocularity which have marked his behaviour hitherto. A witness who knew the accused as a fellow-workman ten years ago deposed that he went with his mates under the nickname of the demon. In the evidence of another witness the name of the unhappy woman whose body was found at Rainhill Was tnentioned for the first time in the 'present inquiry, the pliofOgmpt of her being identified.

The: " Melbourne Age "publishes a telegram from Sydney stating that Deeming when in business there married a young woman although, his wife and children were living with him in the city. Deeming saw his newly-made wife once or twice a week for about a month and then deserted her. The woman recognised Deeming's description pub:ished in the newspapers as being that of the man she married although under an- other name. Inquiries says the" Age" confirm these statements and show that the bridegroom destroyed the- marriage license directly the ceremony was over.

A. MISSIONARY FOR THE POLICE COURTS. On Tuesday afternoon a meeting was held at the Masonic Rooms, Sankey-st., Warrington, in conneo- tion with 6` The Clarke Aspinall Temperance Memorial for appointing 'lye more police court missionaries to labour in Liverpool and in the large - - towns in the diocese of Liverpool." It has been decided by the Memorial Committee to commence a special fund for the maintenance of a police court missionary to labour in Warrington, Widnes, and Newton, under the direction of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society. The Rector of Warring- ton presided over a small audience, which included the Rev. Canon Whitley (rural dean), the Rev. Canon Blundell (rector of Halsall and rural dean of Ormskirk), the Rev. J. J. Langliam, the Rev. T. W. Cook. the Rev. J. Hire!. (diocesan secretary),the Rev. C. E. Jackson, the Rev. J. Shirtcliffe, Mr. R.. Garnett, Mr. J. Faircleugh, Mrs. Willis, and Mrs. J. Pierpoint ; Mr. W. C. Proctor (treasurer, Liverpool). The liscroa read letters apologizing for the absence of the Rev. Canon Penrhyn (Winwick), the Rev. R. C. E. Carleton (Warrington), and the Rev. I. M. Mitchell (Burtonwoo l). He remarked there were many strong reasons why they should meet that day. He, for one, was much indebted to Mr. Aspinall, for during the three years he had lived in Warrioren he had addressed three meetings in their-06611.66m. He was pleased to hear from Mr. Hirst that the fund for the benefit of Mrs. Aspinall had been cloud, the required amount having been collected. (Applause.) Mr. Aspinall did not leave. a large sum behind him. He gave his income away freely for the promotion of objects he had at heart. If the fund had not been closed lie would have been very,' sorry if their efforts had acted prejudicially to its success- ful accomplishment. He was sure that the present form of memorial would have gratified Mr. Aspinall. (Applause), ei a —The Rev. Canon BLUNDBLL having addressed ttie trreet, ing, Mr. PROCTOR pointed out that the POliC &nt nais- t.. sionary for Warrington, in addition to bial police court work, would take down the names r those with whom he had bad interviews, and folioTe them to their homes. In the cesu of those who 'Were committed to prison, fewer than Liverpool 7,,3 tooo free men would visit them en their return to town and e tiitabilexyr given sa id at that Walton, nn could tell the extent of the good which might be done. one . one bTherea rays breakfasts had . Jm and women on the discharge, dan they frequently came into contact with Warrington p tiene convicted tor drunkenness, and that was one 01 the t reasons which induced them to take l case of Warring- ton into consideration They -wanted a man who would b. useful as a missionary and woul deal have a great as a speaker, and as he of trave!ling, to do, it was thought that they would require a sum of £l5O per year. LB —The Rev. Canon WRIT Y moved:—" That this meet- in.' having heard from the deputation representing the Clarke Aspinall Temperance Memorial Committee a des- cription of the work of the Police Court Mission, heartily approves of the proposal to appoint a missionary for the Warrington, Widnes, and Newton Police Courts, and trusts it will receive the liberal pecuniary support of the public." (An,.. plause.)—Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH seconded, and the. Rev. J. L LANEMA3I supported the motion.—Mr. ROBEZEI, Gilman, who was asked to speak by the Chainnan,said a police court missionary was required, but hardly in.the.. form which had been presented to the meeting that doq. He did not care to go shares with Whines and Nes.r.,on in the matter. They wanted a man or a woman therrwlves. A woman might be obtained in Warrington who would be . worth half -a-dozen men to do the work for £2O er_£3o a year, and who would do the work admirably. At the same time, he should not care to oppose the mc,tion before . the meeting.—lt was decided to put the resolution to the meeting, and it was carried unanimously.A sub-corn- _ mittee was appointed to collect subscriptions, namely, the Rev. Canon Whitler, the Rev. G. U. Garrett, the Rey, I. Hirst, the Rev. J. J. Langham, the Rector, and Mr. John Fairclough.

west, north, and south to staying at home and taking a full townsman's share in the work of im- Povmg the town. No; he is not the man for Warrington. There are too many wealthy idlers in Parliament. A thriving commercial town must for the future have as its representative a man of industry, energy, proved capacity, and high charac- ter; in short, it must have Dr. Housrox.

Brunner IT was a matter of course that Mr. for J. T. BRUNNER, the present mem- ber for the Northwich Division of Cheshire, should again be adopted as the Liberal candidate ; and it was equally a matter of course that he should be adopted with enthusiasm. The meeting of the General Council, at Northwicb, an Saturday, WU largely attended, and there was every evidence of eagerness for the fray. The erectors have now had no little experience of the quality of their representative; and they have found that it is a quality which is in every way to their liking. Mr. BRUNNER is not content to beat time as a Liberal; he is always in the van of pro- gress, and that is to say he is always on the side of !Ile people. His time and his purse are freely used In.promoting all good objects; and it would be a iiusfortune to the constituency, if he did not con- tittle to be its representative. Not that there is any fear of a change—unless the Liberals make the mis- -12,41"3 of treating Mr. Whiteley, the Tory candi- mate, as of no moment. It is true that he is out for the purpose of having what may be called a politi- " spree " ; and that—if report speaks correctly --he is to have all the fun of the fair without being called on to pay the piper. It is perhaps diffi- cult therefore to regard him as aserious:opponent ; II", on the other hand, it must be remembered that he is pledged to give the Tories a good run for their money; and that, as his ambition is of the vaulting kind, he will run in—if he can. What the Liberals have got to do is to give Mr. Whiteley , tich a beating that he will refuse for the future to Pc used as a catspaw—particularly when there are a, ()chestnuts to be had from the fire. He has made 31. known that if he gets a seat in Parliament he will watch the interests of "the trade," and !lack up an effete policy of compensating arewers. A politician who takes such a stand, after the people of this country have twice pro- fled against compensation, may be said to mock the desires and interests of the working-class. Ria interests are not their interests, and they may be quite sure that in serving "the trade" he is not IP. mindful that he will be serving a certain brewer IP Blackburn from whom he has great expectations. 4.1". BRUNNER has fought a hard fight against cora- Delegation ; and he is ready, if need be, to fight %gale. He has set himself the task of giving publi- LtPli a fair chance by seeking to abolish, or at any Tate diminish, the evils of the tied-house system ; While on all questions affecting the interests of the Workers he has shown that he is earnest, 'helpful, led.practical. He is looking forward to the oppor- tunitx of assisting in the social legislation which !ill characterise the next Parliament ; and it is teethe electors to see to it that the opportunity is %treaded him.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The pipe across the Mersey at Fiddler's Ferry is evidently not "the pipe of peace"; it is more likely to result in pieces of pipe, for, although only just completed, it has become useless through the effect of rapid tides and currents.

The question—" Is life worth living? " seems to have been settled in the negative in Roumania, where five young military men have taken their lives as members of a Suicide Club. De Quincey once had something to say about " murder as a fine art" ; but a Suicide Club was beyond even his fertile imagination.

The Vicar of Burtonwood's complaint that the Church is "as damp as a vault" recalls the story of the bishop who was called upon to preach special sermons under like circumstances. He had occasion to speak in strong terms of what he called "the damp old church." Imagine his horror when he found that a local paper had reported him as condemning "the damned old church."

In London a property owner named W. A. Murphy has been heavily fined by a stipendiary magistrate, for neglecting to comply with an order to put a house of his in Camberwell in a proper condition. What makes the case worse is that he is a member of the ruling authority in the district of the insanitary property. There is nothing extraordinary in this, except the fact that, through the determination of the magistrate, the charge has been brought home to the offender.

It has been suggested that persons guilty of glaring breaches of the Public Health Act should be disqualified from representing the ratepayers on any ruling authokity. This would sweep away many Town Councillors,and some Aldermen—that is if steps were taken to show them up as offen- ders. But "there's the rub." They sit on Com- mittees, and wink at each other's misdoings, and treat warning notices as so much waste paper. Why don't working-men bestir themselves in such matters P They and their families are the greatest suffewers.

Some important evidence was given, on Monday, before a House of Commons Committee on the question of Shop Hours. Dr. Richardson and Dr. Norman Kerr were quoted 83 stating that long shop hours were alike injurious to women and their offspring. It was admitted that the Shop Hours Regulation Bill of 1884 had done some good; but it was urged that something more ought to be done. The Half-holiday having been secured in this district, every effort should now be made to obtain early closing.

There is a place for everything, but the place for a barbed wire fence is not by the side of a public footpath. It is being "tried on" by the footpath which runs through Windle Hall Farm; and it is perhaps as well that the owner should know that he is responsible at law for any injury to dress or person which may be caused thereby. Indeed if a flesh wound had to result in death from blood-poisoning, it might end in a verdict of man- slaughter. That barbed wire fence is out of place; it should be taken down immediately.

At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Peter Colman, a boy of 13, was sent to prison for ten days for stealing three bricks valued at threepence. The sentence is out of all proportion to the offence, and, taking the age of the offender into account, it will be generally regarded as shockingly severe. It was ordered, too, that the lad should be afterwards sent to a Reformatory for five years. Presumably he has a bad record; but let it not be forgotten that his crime in this .case was stealing three bricks.

The financial year for Warrington comes round again with the usual result so far as Longford is concerned—more money lost and more money wanted. Need anyone be surprised that there is to be an increase in the rates ? The French went into the war with Germany " with a light heart;" and Alderman Burgess has so much of the Frenchman in him that he is lightest of heart when Longford shows the largest deficiency.

The Chairman of the Sanitary Committee al- ways talks as if Longford Works made money rather than lost it; but Councillor F. A. Roberts I demonstrated a loss of £l,OOO per year upon Long- ford as a manufactory pure and simple. There was no gainsaying the figures; and Councillor H. Roberts, a member of the Sanitary Committee, ad- mitted the loss of £l,OOO a year, at the same time arguing that the money was well spent. But there's the admission—a loss of £l,OOO per year!

Councillor Shaw aven did quite right to call attention to a system adopted at one school in Warrington of inflicting fines of Id. on children who are absent. The same thing is done at a Runcorm school. As there is no warrant in law for taking such an extraordinary course, it is a matter of courso to say that it is illegal. It is— not to put too fine a point on it—an unjust impo- sition ; and parents may safely refuse to pay the fine. We shall never have Free Education if such a method of snatching a fee is to be tolerated.

'When will Parliament dissolve That is the question everybody is asking ; but nobody can get a satisfactory answer. Perhaps, as Mr. Glad- stone said the other evening, the Government themselves don't know. They are waiting for what they regard as the right moment, and the right moment doesn't show itself. They are in the position of the young orator, who floundered in and on, with his father in the chair. Seeing the audience getting weary, the father whispered, during a pause enforced by application to a glass of water—" Say a good thing Jimmy, and sit down." "Yes," said Jimmy, " that's what I have been trying to do."

In the same way the Government are striving after their" good thing," and they flounder on and on until the whole country is tired of them. Still, they must dissolve before long, though they may play the trick of appealing to the country on a worn-out register' knowing that such a register is I unfavourable to the working-classes, who are most subject to removals. A return just issued shows that July stands to the front as the month for dissolutions • and rightly or wrongly, the impress- ion is abroad even amongst the Tories that the General Election will take place soon after Whitsuntide.

The motto for the Liberals must be "Ready, aye ready." In Warrington the Tories are at work canvassing; and,as will be seen from another column, reply post cards are being sent out, asking voters to pledge themselves for Mr. Robert Pier- point. If they are wise, they will do nothing of the kind; they will want to know what Mr. Robert Pierpoint is going to do for them. They will con- trast his blank programme, and barren criticism, with the full programme and fertile speeches of Dr. Houston, and, if they have half an eye, they they will say—" Houston s the man for Warring- ton."

Touching Tory tactics, here are the particulars of a thoroughly characteristic incident: A well- known Liberal met two Tories at work this week in the neighbourhood of Bank Quay. Knowing one of them the Liberal said :—" Well you are electioneering, I see."—Tory : " Yes, for want of a better job; and I could do with a better for this chap with me wants a pint at every corner." How suggestive of what may continue to happen Let working-men beware of the pint and stick to principle. Why not canvass each other in the workshsp and the street? If over there was a time when workmen should look to their inter- ests—it is now—now whilst history is in the making.
WESTON BIBLE AND MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.

On Tuesdoy night last the annual meeting, which closes the session, was held hi the Wesleyan schoolroom. Songs, readings, &c., were given by several of the members, and a pleasant eveniag was spent. Mr. James Ford was re-elected President of the class.

On Thursday afternoon the memorial stones of the Parochial Room for St. Paul's district of Widnes parish were laid, in the presence of a large assembly, by Mrs. T. Sutton Timmis and Mrs. Deacon. The estimated cost is about £3,000, of which £2,000 has been raised, includ• ing a donation of £6OO from Mr. T. Sutton Till3Mig.
POLICI INSPICTION AT W/DNIS.

On Wednesday afternoon, Sir Herbert Croft, Bart., Government inspector of police, held an inspection at Widnes. There were 28 constables and six sergeants on parade. Superintendent Keighley and Inspector Pattinson were also present. The various acccutrements of the officers, as well as the books, &c., were examined, and the inspector expressed his pleasure at finding everything n first-rate order. Ass ACCIDINT AT FAINTON foci Yin?mom. At the Liverpool:Assizes, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Collins, an action to recover damages for negligent tow- age was heard. The plaintiffs were Messrs. Robinson and Co., and the defendants the Manchester Ship Canal Company.—The captain of the barge having given evi- dence, his lordship said that the Helen might have been the cause of the collision, but the action was not brought in respect of that tug.—Mr. Kennedy applied to have the particular. arnended.—His lordship permitted this on plaintiffs paying costs of that trial.

div.p: BRUTAL KICKING CASK AT '

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Francis Gay- nor, of Ellison-st., was brought up on remand charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounded his wife. The dying depositions of the woman have been taken, and show that she has been subject to constant cruelty at her husband's hands. On Saturday night he threatened to "finish her," and beat and kicked her in a most in- human maaner. He several times lifted her by the hair and then dashed her to the ground and kicked her. Dr. Hudson said the woman was in a very dangerous con- dition, and the ptisoner was again remanded.

div.head: IHSPRCTION OF POLICE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: IHSPRCTION OF POLICE AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday afternoon, Sir Herbert, H.M. Inspector of Constabulary, inspected the police force of the Runcorn Division. There were on parade Superintendent Ather- ton, Inspector Cooper, 4 sergeants, and 21 constables. There were five constables absent on duty, and one ser- geant and one constable sick. The men were put through a number of military evolutions, and the Inspector ex- pressed his approval of the -mart appearance of the men, and the manner in which they had gone through their drill. The Inspector also inspected the building through- out, and carefully examined the books, and everything was found to be highly satisfactory.

TDB MARRIAOR OF PROFESSOR H. LLOYD SEAM County Alderman and Mrs. Thomas Snap° (of Liver- pool and Widnes) held an " At Home" and garden party at "The Gables," Crowteth-road, on Monday afternoon, the raison d'etre being the recent marriage with Miss Maud Mary Allen, sebond daughter of the late Mr. John B. Allen, ot Norwich, of their son, Professor Hy. Lloyd Snipe. D.Sc., Ph. D., professor of chemistry at .tieryst- with University College. The guests were received by Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Snape, and by them were intro- duced to Professor and Mrs. Lloyd Snaps. The gather- ing was of a very social and interesting character, fur- ther enhanced by the polite attentions to the guests of Miss Mabel M. and Miss S. Gertrude Snape. The nume- rous and pretty wedding presents were shown. In the dining-room and in the summer house in the garden the physical needs of visitors were consulted, and music at intrvals was provided.

He still continues to collect the offertory each Sunday, but no doubt the crisis will be reached on Easter Monday. CO-OPBRA.TIVE FlBIl SUPPLY COMPANY.

This Company has ita centre at Grimsby, with an establishment at Billingsgate Buildings, London. It has been very successful in meeting the wants of families throughout the country who desire to have a cheap supply of fish direct from the landing stage. Indeed the Company has had to apply to the High Court to restrain an unscrupulous imitator. Mr. Justice Chitty in granting a restraining order, commented strongly on the fraud that was being attempted ; and gave costs against the defendants. It will be well therefore for customers to make sure that they are dealing with the original Company. An advertisement giving particulars will be found in another column.

UMBAELLLS RECOVERRD.—J. and W. Durros,, Sankey-t., 1 Warrington.—Advt. PRESCOT AND THB COUNTY COUNCIL. The bye-election to fill the vacancy caused by Mr. W. L. M'Clure's election as Alderman of the Lanca- shire County Council, took place on Saturday, the candidates being Mr. E. J. Grimshaw, mining en- gineer, Duyton and St. Helens, and Mr. Thomas Dobell, farmer, Wheat Hill, Gateacre. The contest was somewhat one-sided, through a rumour that Mr. Dobell had withdrawn two days previous to the day of the poll. The poll upened at eight o'clock, but the voting was slow until the afternoon. At five minutes to ten o'clock the deputy returning officer, Mr. Castle Spencely, announced the figures: —Edward J. Grimshaw, 708; Thomas Dobell, 55; majority, 653; and declared Mr. Grimshaw elected. 1 BASSI Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Bariestown.

A meeting of the Blackburn Town Council was held on Wednesday night to till up the vacant town- clerkship. Mr. 11. E. Fox, town-clerk of Burnley, was appointed, at a salary of .£l.OOO a year. Mr. Fox was admitted solicitor in 1833, and after prac- tising in Liverpool and in Warrington, in the office of Messrs. R. The Coroner cautioned the witness, who repeated that he did not see any kicking.—Richard Jones, labourer, and Ann Baker, Mersey-at., also gave evidence.—Mr. Knowles then called James Ganner, Ship Canal labourer, of I, Water-st., who said a bother arose in the street between two strange persons. Witness got between them to take Rawlinson away, but deceased followed him up and struck him again. Then they fought together. Twice they fell, and he helped them to their reek and at last the deceased jumped back to avoid a blow from Rawlinson, tripped his feet against the curbstone, and fell with the back of his head against the parapet. Ile lay there unconscious, and witness lifted him up and carried him home. Dr. McDougall said he was called to the deceased on the 16th of March, his assistant, Dr. Peart, having seen the case and prescribed for him on the previous day. lie found him in bed quite conscious and rational. lie examined him carefully and found a slight bruise above the left ear. By order of the coroner he made a post mortem etamination of the body on Saturday afternoon last. In his opinion death was due to the pressure of an abscess on the convolu- tions of the brain, consequent on a fracture of the base of the skull.—Bv the Coroner: lie did not think a blow from a clog would produce such injury,it was most likely done by falling heavily on some projection in the street. —Susan Pilling, widow of the deceased, said her hus- band complained that some men all got on to him •nd kicked him from one end of the street to the other.—The

jury returned the following verdict :—" Death resulted from injuries received in a street row."—The prisoner Rawlinson was brought before Mr. G. L. Davies at Run. corn Police Court on Wednesday, and discharged for want of evidence.

A friendly match, between a tram from Hartford and a team selected from the Runcorn Volunteer Shooting Club, took place at Runcorn Heath on Saturday. Each captain brought twelve men on the ground, the ten best scores to count. The weather was very fine, but the entire absence of wind made against the scores, as the smoke from the rifles hung on the ground to such an extent as to almost entirely obscure the targets, especially at long distances. AT RUNCORN, &c.

BY AN Occ &stoma'. CORRIISPONDRNT. The gathering of the Liberal Council at Northwich on Saturday was one of the largest and most repre- sentative that has been held for some years past. Instead of the advent of the much vaunted Mr. George Whiteley having caused fear and consterna- tion in the party, the members were full of enthus- iasm, and, as Mr. Brunner observed,absolutely spoil- ing for a fight. In fact they hail the contest with and as an occasion for keeping their armour bright and their forces in line. The secretary, Mr. Handley, had a favourable report of the past year's operations to submit, and the appointment of officers was rapidly settled. In placing Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., of Runcorn, on the list of representatives to the National Federation, Mr. Fletcher referred to the withdrawal of that gentleman's membership from the Association, and both he and Mr. Norman deplored the circumstances which had occasioned it. The meeting unanimously passed a resolution asking Mr. Speakman to reconsider his communication, and there is every reason to believe that Mr. Speakman will continue to identify himself officially with the party with which he has been so long associated in the work of progress and reform.

I have frequently heard Conservatives describe Mr. Brunner's popularity as on the wane, but there was no evidence of this on Saturday, and I think the wish is father to the thought on the part of our friends the enemy. The resolution adopting Mr. Brunner as the candidate was received with an enthusiasm seldom equalled in meetings of this de- scription, and when Mr. Brunner afterwards entered the room, there was a tremendous demonstration of the hold which Mr. Brunner has upon the affec- tion and minds of his supporters. In acknowledging the vote and the ovation, Mr. Brunner touched upon several needful reforms, and expressed the hope that the coming contest would be a fair, open, straight- forward fight, and no hitting below the belt.

To Mr. Brunner the word thorough may be applied in every sense. He has been a close student of the history of his country, is deeply read in political economy, and is in touch with the desires and as- pirations of the people. His speeches may not be eloquent,but they are characterised by deep thought and an unmistakable wish and intention to uplift his fellow-men in the scale of humanity. And when the time comes for the electors of Northwich Divi- sion to express their opinion at the ballot box,these things will be remembered, while Mr. Whiteley's "airy nothings" and musty anecdotes will be for- gotten.

The block of property which Mr. P. Speakman is erecting at the corner of Savage's Bridge,and which I suppose may appropriately be named "Speakman's Buildings" is likely to be of a most important char- acter. The Post Office, the ldanchester and Salford Bank, and the Liberal Club are to find a home there, and accommodation is also provided for several suites of offices,so that we may expect "Speakman's Building," to be a chief centre of business. There will also be a number of first-class shops.

The result of the County Council election at Widnes, on Saturday, displayed most unmistak- ably the folly of the Tory party opposing Mr. Deacon, who in every way was so wall qualified to fill the office. Let us hope his majority on this occasion is prophetic of victory when the more im- portant contest arrives, and that Mr. Deacon may add M.P. to the C.C. which now follows his name.

The proposal to pay jurymen for their services at Widnes seems likely to fall through, because the Railway Companies and the Alkali Company decline to contribute to the voluntary rate. As these Companies are the largest ratepayers, and it is on their works the great majority of fatal accidents occur, it is only reasonable that they should provide a share to the fund. However, as retaliation Superintendent Keighley has been re- quested by a meeting of ratepayers to call upon the employds of these companies to serve upon juries, duty from which they are practically exempt at the present time.

The grocers' assistants of Runcorn are very likely to obtain the desired half-holiday. Out 0129 mas- ters 26 have signed a memorial favourable to the holiday, and there are strong hopes entertained that the other three will give way.

div.head: SHOCKING SEQUEL TO A STREET FIGHT
div.p: SHOCKING SEQUEL TO A STREET FIGHT
AT RUNCORN.
THE COMBATANTS TOO DRUNK TO STAND.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner for the honour and fee of Halton, OR Saturday morning opened an inquest at Runcorn Police Court on the body of Frederick Filling, of 11, Sutton-street, who died on Thursday afternoon from the effects of injuries rece ved on the 12th March, during street brawl. Mr. C. Dutton was foreman of the jury.—Matthew John Sweetman, coal dealer, Malcolm-street, identified the deceased, and said he was 29 years of age. He was a mechanics' labourer on the Ship Canal.—After this evid- ence the Coroner gave an order for the burial of the deceased and adjourned the inquest until Tuesday, when the jury again aslSembled in the Police Court.—Mr. Superintendent Atherton was present for the police and I Mr. J. W. Knowles (Widnes) represented Thomas Raw- linson, who was present in custody, being on remand by the magistrates charged with unlawfully wounding the ' deceased.—Jessie Wood, 1, Water-street, said on the night of the 12th March she heard deceased challenge Rawllnson to fight, and also say that he would fight the "best—lrish man in the Rookery." Both men were very drunk. They fought, deceased striking the first blow. There was no kicking and no weapons used ; but the men kept falling, and were both bleeding from the nose and the mouth. She saw the deceased fallbackwards on the back of his head on the parapet. James Irvine, 31, Suffolk-street, night watchman, said the two men were on the ground wrestling together when he got to the place, and Pilling had to be carried Off a short time afterwards. The men were down twice, for he heard the "bump" when he was on the other side of the rails. The men were not very drunk, so far as he could see.—By Superintendent Atherton: He had made a statement to Sergeant Woolley whinh was quite different to what he now said ..—The Coroner : Why is it different ?—,-Witness: I did not have a proper recol- lection; I had to mind over what he had seen.—The Coroner : When did you make the statement ?—Witness: Monday night.—Superintendent Atherton: It was on the 23rd.—Mr. Knowles said he must object to these ques- tions ; it was like cross-examining their own witness.— The Coroner : I shall not allow you to object to anything I do in this court.—Mr. Knowles : But Mr. Coroner— The Coroner : You are here by my permission, and I shall not allow you to object—Mr. Knowles: Don't you think—The Coroner: 1 shall not allow an objection. The witness in answer to further questions, said he men- tioned kicking to Sergeant Woolley.—The Coroner: Was

CANAL BOAT CHILDREN.

At the meeting of the School Attendance Committee on the 29th March, 42 parents were summoned; 35 appeared. Proceedings were ordered to Iye taken against 16 parents. The monthly returns of the visitors showed an increase of 164 in the number on the rolls, and 116 in the averare attendance. The Committee had under their consideration the bad attendance of children who were taken away on canal beats, and recommended that printed notices be distributed to boat people informing them that in future the Board would not accept as a reasonable excuse the plea that childrenmere taken away on boats, but would insist on the regular attendance at school of all children of school age.—The minute was passed on the motion of Dr. Gastaldi, seconded by Mr. Salkeld.

div.head: Total for Runoorn Showing a balance in favour of Runcorn of 144 points.
div.p: Total for Runoorn Showing a balance in favour of Runcorn of 144 points.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. Mr..). Pritchard presided, and there were present Rev. Canon Maitland Wood. Rev. Dr. GesteMi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Handley, A. Salk,ld, and S. Taylor, with G. Moss (clerk).
INO /ARAM OF SALARY.

The School Management Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. E. W. Rosser, assistant master at Greenway-road Boys' School, be advanced to ZOO per annum, and that the salary of Miss M. A. Perkins, certi- ficated assistant mistress at Greenway-road Girls' School, be advanced to £5O per annum, both dating from May Ist. EXTRA PEES AT TRINITY SCHOOLS.

At the meeting of the School Attendance Committee, on March Btb, 48 parents were summoned and 43 ap- peared. Several parents pleaded that their children, on presenting themselves at Trinity Schools, had been sent home for extra fees on account of having attended badly, and rather than pay they had kept their children at home. The Committee doubt whether these extra fees are legal,and would be reluctant to prosecute the parents, as it is probable the magistrates would not grant a con- viction under the circumstances. The difficulty is one of long standing, and formed the subject of a correspon- dence with the Education Department, in January, 1885. when the Department requested the managers of -Trinity Schools to discontinue the practice alluded to. The Committee recommended that a letter be written to the Education Department, stating the facts, and asking for guidance in the matter. Mr. Handley moved the adoption of the minute, and said it seemed to bathe rule at Holy Trinity School to charge double fees to children who were irregular in their attendance. This was a serious stumbling block, in getting children to school, and it seemed to the com- mittee that the parents had a lair argument for not sending their children to school.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion.—Canon Wood asked was it not usually con- sidered a matter of courtesy to communicate with the managers of schools concerned, before taking such an extreme step as writing to the Education department. Had a communication been sent.—Mr. Handley : A com- munication was sent in 1885.—Canon Wood : That is some time ago.—Dr. McDougall said he hoped the Board would never commit itself to what would be unquestion- ably one of the most injudicious, indecorous, and uncourteous methods if conducting business that could be adopted by a body of public representatives. It was a far cry to go back to 1885. Things had altered since that date. They had assisted Education to the extent of 10s. given to these schools, and the Board did not know to what extent the Trinity managers were justi- fied in the course they had taken. There was nothing before them but the statement of several parents, and the proper way was to communicate with the correspon- dent of the managers.—Mr. Salkold agreed with this course being adopted, because tne cases brought before the school attendance committee had been very bad ones ' indeed. In one case the woman had been in prison, she had been fined four times, and for five months had never sent her children to school, and the managers had some grounds for charging the extra fee.—Mr. Taylor said when the parents made those state- ments, the Committee felt that no bench of magistrates would convict,and what were the Committee to do? The children were not attending school,and,in his opinion the high-handed course adopted at Trinity schools was very detrimental to the work of that Board.—Canon Wood moved that the Clerk be instructed to send an official com- munication on the subject of extra fees said to be charged by the managers of Trinity Schools to the correspon- dent of the schoole.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded.—Mr. Hand- ley disclaimed any intention to be discourteous and said he would accept the amendment.—Canon Wood said if they wanted to get on with people they must not begin by threatening them, and it was to the interest of all concerned that it should be arranged without difficulty. —Mr. Taylor : The question is do they make these extra charges. There was never anything done yet but people had da reason for it.—Mr. McDougall said if these people had the right of doing this they must show the reason why they had recourse to it and in what manner they had exercised it.—The Chairman agreed with writing to the managers, whose intention, he said, was no doubt to get constant and regular attendance, but the effect was the very contrary. It had a tendency to exclude children from school because parents decidedly objected to paying extra fees, and they had a legitimate excuse afforded them for not sending their children to school. If fines were wrong seven years ago when fees were charged throughout the country it was a far worse and more glaring thing now in the days of free educ- ation. The other day the son of the Premier said any parent who desired could demand and get free education for his child, the authorities would have to make provi- pion for the demand made upon them. If that were so it was it mistaken policy on the part of school managers to charge extra lees, and would not receive the sanction of the Education Department. Ultimately it was de- cided that the clerk should send to the managers of Trinity School a letter similar to that which he would have sent to the Education Department, and the discus- sion ceased. MORN SCHOOL ACCOMODATION WANTBD.

Visitor Bowyer brought forward a list of 5 or 6 children of school age residing in Newtown who were not attend- ing school, owing to Newtown Infant School being full. The parents were unwilling to send the children to infant schools in the lower part of the town, and the Committee suggested that the Board take into considera- tion the provision of more school accomodation for infants In the district named.—ln moving the adoption of this minute, Mr. Handley said Newtown was a growing dis- trict, and it was important that the Board should immediately consider the provision of more accomoda- tion. He moved that the subject be referred to the School Management Committee.—Mr. McDougall pointed out that there was now an extremely good road from Greenway-road to Mill Brow and there was a possibility of extending Mill Brow School to meet what may be required. He thought the subject had better be def Ted. The Clerk said there were now 16 children not going to school.—lt was decided to refer the question to a Com- mittee of the whole Board.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

The Clerk submitted a petition he had received from the Central Association for stopping the sale of intoxicat- ing liquors on Sunday. in favour of the Sunday Closing Act.—Mr. Handley moved, Dr. Gastaldi seconded, and Canon Wood supported a motion that the Chairman sign the petition on behalf of the Board. Only these gentle- men voted; the remainder remaining neutral.—The Chairman signed the petition. TEACHICRS' TUNIS CLUB.

An application was read from the head master and head mistress of Greenway-road School for permission to use the play ground of the school for tennis in the evenings. The matter was referred to the School Management Committee.

div.head: RUNCORN ROA RD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN ROA RD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of members was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday, Mr. J. ()rice presided and there were present Messrs. IL White,J. Meadow- croft, J. W. Lightburn, IL Abel, W. Timmins, .9. Coward, E. W. Humphreys, D. Bisbrown, F. Wis- wall, S. Tavlor, J. Pritchard, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor) and Dr. McDougall (medical officer.)

MERSEY BRIDGE COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that this Board joins the Widnes Local Board in the expense of taking COUR. eel's opinicn as to the liabilities of the L. and N.W. Railway Co. with regard to the Ferry, and that it pay the cost thereof. Mr. Wiswall moved and Mr. Taylor seconded the adoption of the minutes.—ln reply to Mr. Meadowcroft, the Law Clerk said the case for counsel's opinion would be prepared jointly by Mr. Oppenheim and himself,and he did not think the total cost would be more than £5 ss.—Carried. THE WORK AND REFERRER OF THE COMING YEAR. The Finance Committee recommended that the esti mates of the money required for the year ending March 25th, 1893, be approved, Estimated expenditure £6,521. Estimated income £6BO. Amount required £5,841. That a general district rate at the rate of 2s. 4d. in the £ for the year ending 25th March, 1693, be made; and that is. 2d. be collected in the fint ell months and is. 2d. in the second six months, With respect to the assessment and levying of the geTtere district rate for the year end- ing 25th March, 1893, it is recornitended that the owner instead of the occupier, be rated, tttider the provision of 211 of the Public Health Act, 1876, where the rateable value if any premises liable to assessment does not ex- ceed the sum of tetv pounds, and that he be assessed on a reduced estimate of three-fourths of the net annual value of such property.—Mr. Taylor moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Bisbrown seconded the motion.—The minutes were adopted.
Urrll-11 11111911 Y coinasszowins.

aMr , Wilma proposed that Mr. Samuel Taylor be ap- pointed to represent the Board on the Upper Mersey Navi- gation Commission for the ensuing three years, and that the seal of the Board be affixed to the deed of appoiht- inente--Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion with pleasure and it was carried unanimously, and Mr. Taylor suitably acknowledged the honour conferred upon him.

SUNDAY CLOSING. TfrE geetelt ary submitted a petition forwarded by the CO/KM Association for stopping the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday, in favour of the Sunday Closing Bill.— Ile. Bisbrown moved that the petition be adopted. He laid it was not at all a party:question. It transcended in interest either party, class, or creed, and :the benefits arising from universal Sunday closing would be simply incalculable. The publicans themselves were in favour of it. Some few years ago the publicans were canvassed on the subject and with the exception of three or four they were in favour of Sunday Closing. Taking the country through there were seven householders to one in favour of the measure, and petitions in favour of the measure Riad been adopted by 500 School Boards, 117 Local Boards, a number of Town Councils, 350 Boards of Guardians and 14 .County Councils ; and he urged the Commissioners to follow a similar course.—Mr. E. W. Humphreys formally seconded the motion.—Mr. Meadowcroft moved that the subject be referred to the Parliamentary Committee for consideration and to obtain information on the question.—Mr. Wiswall seconded and said these publicans who were in favour of Sunday closing could deal with matter them- selves by asking for six days licenses.—The Chairman supported and expressed the hope that the Committee would go into the matter. The amendment was cartied by a large majority, only Mr. Bisbrown and Mr. Humph- reys voting for the motion.—On the amendment being put as a substantive motion. Mr. Humphreys moved that the Parliamentary Committee be instructed to re- port to a special meeting to be held that day week.— Mr. Wiswall seconded the amendment.—Mr. Taylor explained that he had declined to vote because he con- sidered the question outside the province oi the Board.— Mr. Humphreys said having accomplished his object he would withdraw his amendment. THE CLOSING OF RUNCORN DOCKS. Mr. Lightburn explained the position with reeardlto the proposed deep dock Nu. Runcorn. He stated that on February 11th a deputation from the Board waited upon the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal, when they had under consideration the provision of a daep dock, or a lay by ; the customs arrangements, which were about to be altered, removing them from Runcorn to Liverpool ; a matter of drainage, which thou:h to a certain extent of a private character, was important to the ratepayers of the town; and the keeping open of the docks at Runcorn during the construction of the canal. With regard to the deep dock, they had not re- ceived a reply, but if this were not provided they might with confidence expect to have a lay-by. With regard to the Customs House removal, that was to remain in its present form. As to the closing of the docks, that sub- ject was under their censideration,and they had a scheme of their own, to be determined upon at a later period. They had decided to close the docks temporarily for the more expeditious carrying on of the works in the neigh- bourhood, and for bringing to a completion at an earlier date the deeper waterway between Runcorn and the sea. The question arose what was Runcorn to do in the mean- time. He believed the arrangements were that Weston Dock and Weaver Pool would be used as the place of discharge, and that the goods would be brought thence, to the Runcorn warehouses, so that there would be a body of men working at the two places, which would necessi- tate a double handling of cargoes,and consequently cause increased labour. The men would be paid at Runcorn, as usual. With respect to seamen and those who traded with them, arrangements would be made for the carrying ing of the goods from Runcorn to Weston free of charge. It was the desire of the Ship Canal Company to put the traders in the same position as they new occupied, and be was told that some of those most closely interested were perfectly satisfied with the proposed arrangements. He trusted the good feeling which had existed between the Board and the Ship Canal Company would be continued, sii,l if they could de anything to improve the position of r fie inhabitants of the town they would only be too glad. Mr. Meaelowcroft said if the directors thought it was advisable to close the entrance at Runcorn it would be ' at an enormous cost to them, and the only object in doing it would be to hasten the opehing of the canal Some months earlier than otherwise might be the case which would be of considerable advantage to the town. Mr. Pritchard considered the remarks very satisfactory.

THE STANDING ORDERS. Mr. numphreys gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that an alteration be made in Standing Order 10, whereby it should not be deemed that a seconder of a resolution,without remarks, had exercised his right to spaak on any subject.

div.head: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.

The Spring General Quarter Sessions for the county were opened at Knutsford Sessions House, on Monday, his Honour Sir Horatio Lloyd (chairman) presiding in the first court, and Mr. Charles Lister in the second court. Mr. Henry Lathbury, of Bolton-in-Fee, was foreman of the grand jury. laroline Gleave for theft at Runcorn, five years' penal servitude. Prisoner, who had been allowed to sit, fell back screaming on receiving sentence. Tberebad been numerous previous convictions against her. Peter Brown, of Macclesfield, described as a medical asaiatant, aged 45, was indicted for having obtained on various occasions quantities of morphia from John Wright and Thomas Duncals. chemists, at Macclesfield, by falsely representing that he was in tiae service of Dr. Rushton. und —Bo over in £5O to be of good behaviour and come up for judgment if called upon, and discharged with a warning. Arthur M'Nally, 72, miner,pleaded guilty to wounding his wife at Dukinfield. He had thrown a doe* weight at her and beaten her with a Pnker and months' hard labour. ha dl John Kelly, 62, tailor,. pleaded guilty to stealing tailors shears at Bosden, near Stockport.—One month's hard labour. John Melia, a boy, for false pretences, at Ashton-on- Mersey, was sent to a reformatory for five years. James Wild, 29,.labourer, pleaded guilty to breaking I Into the dwelling of Jonathan Gres,.at Korthenden.— One month's hard labour.

Thomas Murrough, 18, labourer, indicted for stealing a silk muffler, a number of plants, and a coat, the pro- perty of Joseph Phillips, wasdischarged. Charles Symons, 18, warehouseman, for obtaining from Lilließilvert, at Sale, Zs., by representing that he was collecting for a cricket club, which had no existence was sent for four calendar roxmths' hard labour, haying ' been previously convicted.

James M'Keown, Thomas Monaghan, Thomas Norton, and Thomas Lynham, four youths, indicted for breaking into the shop of James Beauinopt, at Dukinfield, and stealing Ave silk handkerchiefs, were bound over under the First Offenders Act to come up for judgment when called upon, and discharged. John Booth, 29, factory hand and nicture salesman, pleaded guilty to obtaining 14s. 6d. by false pretences ' from his employers, Messrs. Pearson and Adcock, by falsely representing that he had sold certain pictures oa their behalf, and was sentenced to nine months' hard labour. . _
Christopher Bannister, 62, factory worker, for stealing a pair of trousers the goods of Alicia Adamson, two months' hard labour.

Thomas Rodgers, 50, striker, pleaded guilty to break- ing into the dwelling of Reuben Broadhurst, and steal- ing two watches, two chains, a brooch, and E.l ss. id. He had previously served over seven years' penal servi- tude, and was at the time under police supervision. Sent to penal servitude for hve years. Anne Mary Hulme, 13, domestic servant,for obtaining food and lodgings, by false pretences, at Stockport. from Louisa II ulme and Jane Bailey, one month's hard labour.

James Parker, 23, labourer, pleaded guilty to obtain- ing two planed and two chisels by false pretence's at Stockport, the property of A. W. Parkes, and was charged on his own recognisances, under the First Offen- ders Act.

John Potts, 32, formerly police constable, Rode Heath, near Sandbach, was charged with stealinglbs. of cheese, the property of Arthur Bailey, Odd Rode, and was also charged with stealing 21Ibs. copper wire, the property of the National Telephone Company ; and also two rubber tricycle tyres and one lamp, the property of John Cooke. Be was found guilty of stealing the cheese and sent to goal for three months. The retnaiping charges were not gone into.

div.head: RUNCORN CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN CRICKET CLUB.

The annual dinner of the members of this club took place a few days ago under the presidency of Mr. J. It Frith, and there was a good attendance. After dinner,which was presided over by Mr. C.Dut- ton,at Wilson's Hotel, the secretary, Mr. G. S. Frith, submitted the annual report, which showed that last season out of 19 matches played 5 were won, 7 lost, and 7 drawn. Their opponent scored 1,137 runs fer the loss of 157 wickets,an average of 7.242 per wicket, against their score of 1,305 runs for the lose 181 wickets, on average of 8.105.-The Chairman pro- posed success to the Runcorn Cricket Club, and referred to his long connection with the club. He said in the re- port of the past year there was much to encourage them as cricketers, and they only needed to set to work with determination to make the club a brilliant suceess. The toast was coupled with the name of Mr. Harry Wright, the captain, who said he anticipated that the forthcom- ing season would be very successful. They had arranged for some good matches, and had launched out to the ex- tent of enjoying a professional. They had obtained the services of a very good man named J. G. Wilson, of Lancaster, who came to them with excellent testi- monials. He hoped with his assistance and by constant practice, the members of the club might become pro- ecient.-Mr. J. J. W. Potter proposed and Mr. J. H. Weston responded to the toast of " The town and trade." The Chairman proposed "The visitors," and Dr. McKenzie and Mr. G. Connor replied. Other toasts fol- lowed, and a capital programme of music was gone - through. The following are the PIXTURBS FOR THII SEASON, 1892. 1197 ELNYNN. 2ND BLEvsar. 1892 1892. Winnington Park H „ 20, Winnington Park A „ 27, Chester A , 27, Helsby TOWNSHIP MEETING AT WIDNES. ATTACK ON THE SCHOOL BOARD.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of Widnes was held in the overseers' office, on Monday even- ing, and there was a larger attendance than usual. Mr. James White was voted to the chair, and sub- mitted a statement of accounts which showed that the overseers had commenced the year with a balance of £6lB 7s 11d. ; a rate of 2s. had produced £13,194 3s.4d.;bank interest £27 73.93.;t0tal £13,839 19s. The payments had been :—Union and county accounts £9,193 ; School Board precept £3,900 ; registration ex- penses, rent, books. stationery, &c. £233 Bs. 7d. ; balance in hand £513 10s. 51—Mr. Goff, the assistant overseer, said the probable requirements for the corning year were :—Union and county account £9,193; School Board precept £4,500; other erpenses £200; total £13,893. A rate of 2.1. in the £ would produce £13,500, so that, after paying all calls there the probable balance would be £l2O 10s. -M.

The Chairman said that the overseers thought they would be able to manage without increasing the rates although the School Board had demanded £6OO more for the ensuing year. The ratable value of the town- ship, toe, bad decreased during the past year. If the expenses of the School Board went on increasing, and the ratable value of the works decreased, he did not know how the money would be found. They would come upon the poor property owners, in fact, it would ruin many of them. He did not think so large a sum was required to have the Board Schools efficient. If they took the Waterloo-road School as an example, they would And proof for this assertion. These schools were acknowledged to be as efficient as the very best Board iSchool in the place. The cost of this school was £lOO per year, and that was raised by voluntary subscrip- tions. If these schools could be carried on at such a small expense, Ise did not see why the Board Schools should cost so much. He thought there must be a waste somewhere, and that there ought to be regeneration in the affairs of the School Board. The Chairman made a violent attack upon Mr.Danby,cterk to the School Board. —The following were then chosen to be submitted as fit persons to be overseers i—Messrs. White, Neil, Wright, Christie, Pankkurst, Owens, and Midwood. —Mr. White said that the question of paying jurors on coroners' inquests was brought forward some time ago, and it was proposed to levy a voluntary rate, but he pointed out the difficulties of this proposition, as the big ratepayers, the railway companies and the Alkali com- pany had refused to pay such a rate. The opinion of the meeting that the railway companies, and the Alkali Company ought to pay the rate, as most accidents were caused by them, and also that the police ought to summon their servants to serve as jurors a little oftener. Even- tually a proposition was passed urging upon the Superin- tendent of Police to call upon the servants of the railway and alkali companies to serve as jurors.

Pris- er put his hand on the sovereign, and drew it. o“ntrhe, en back, and put it into his pocket. Prisoner afterward& went into the backyard, and witness followed him and asked if Paul was any relation to him. Prisoner said, "Heis my father." Prisoner followed Paul about all the afternoon. From his movements, he suspected the prisoner wanted to rob Paul, and he gave information to the police.—P.C. McGuiness proved apprehending the prisoner, and charged him with stealing the sovereign. when he replied" I know nothing about it." Lines Committee, with travelling from Burton-on-Trent. to Warrington without paying her fare. She stated on sa .1. reaching SVarrington, and her ticket being asked for, "easels iethat she had lost it, and said she was going to Liver- :el L.O pool. She was fined ss. and the fare ss. Bd. -;01 fain CHARGE OF THEFT AT TUBd.RRACHS. leno3 Mr At the Borough, Magistestes' Court. on Wednesday morning, John Kirkham, a militiaman, was charged with stealing from Orford Barraelee, on'Saturday, silver .Spoons, the property ;of. the milipsry authbrities at the •TlLOrford Barracks. Sergeant Phillipson deposed to missing the spoons on Sunday morning :and their being eeeefound in the prisonees qaarterse-ellie was fined 205., including costs. ' • s CHARGE OF,FRAIID AGAINST A dßOClitt. . At the Warrington Bonsugh Police Court, yesterday, X Charles Jeavans Parker, grocer, 87, Manchester-road, was charged with selling bread to Elizabeth Pownall L and Emma Kenwright on the 25th ult., loaves of defi- A _ cient weight. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, ap- peared for the prosecution.—Elizabeth Pownall said she asked for a 41b ; loaf and wee supplied with a loaf, X . was 4id. The defendant did not weigh the loaf.—Emma A Xenwright said' she asked for a 21b loaf, and was sup- " ** plied with on., which was not weighed for which she A paid 2d.—Mr. Plaice, inspector of weights and measures deposed that the 4lb loaf was. Boi short and the 211) 2oz short.—The defendant slid he sold the loaves at 4d. and .kriliX2d. respectively unweiglied, and eid. and2iii weighed, and told the witnesses this. Be could do this according ,0:to the Act.—The Town Clerk said he could not dO so, and pressed for a severe penalty remarking that the -.ease was one of fraud on the poor, and that was the Xeraeanest of frauds.—The Cliairman said the witnesses .111U341 ti- did not ask for a 4.1. era 21 loaf but for a 41b and a 2lb *dna tine loaf,and it was the defendants duty to supply them with Saffe heir loaves of these weights ; and jle was liable for not doing 4 eilel so. He would be fined 204. and costs in each case. blesses CHARGE OF TEALING HARNESS. AST f ,At the Warrington Borough Pelice Court, en Tuesday, leap, John Jackson, carter, and James Atherton, were charged ate with stealing a saddle and other harness, the property of ; Thomas Pilkington, contractor. Mr. Longla.nd, appear- ed on behalf of Mr. A. Browne for the prisoners.—Mr. Pilkington said he had missed several articles from the stables, and on the Thursday night previous he got information that a saddle and other articles ef harness J . ewe were in Johnson's possession. Witness did not knowthat eenee t, Jackson had borrowed the saddle. Atherton had been employed by him and he had oecasionally hired a horse from Jackson. He afterwards' found the articles were esesee eee his.—Atherten admitted lending Jackson a saddle and 0160;1. bridle. Widness did not think Jackson meant to keep the , articles, or that Atherton had any felonious intentioo. , D.S. Monaghan deposed to finding the articles on Monday 4,0 w. „, night in Jackson's stable. Jackson, after stating that he 141, had bought them at sales, ultimately admitted that they ,w ere were Mr. Pilkington's. Atherton subsequently said he had 4-, • lent Jackson them over 12 months since. Mr. Pilkington er • identified the articles as his,, and the prisoners were e taken into custody.—Mr.Longland said Jackson had bor- rowed the articles and he merely continued using them, ' not meaning to keep them. He borrowed the saddle to do work for, Mr. Pilkington. He would not have been eiese likely to do that if he had meant to steal it.—Mr. Pilk- ington said, in answer to the Chairman, that he did not r r, L, ' • wish to press the case. He weuld have lett the harness to Jackson if he had asked for it. —Mr. Longland said Jackson had lent Atherton things and Atherton merely lent in return.—The prisoners were dismissed with a reprimand - CHARGE OF CRUELTY TO A HORSE. At the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, • SanIWS/ Kelsall was charged by Inspector Dowtv, R.S.P.C.A., with cruelly treating a horse on the 25th - and 28th ult. at Burtonwoode Mr. A. Brawne appeared to watch the case on behalf of the owner of the horse, and Mr. Forshaw defended.—Williarn Sedgewick, pro- • prietor of an American menagerie, said last autumn when in Warrington he let the defendant have a horse , to keep. It was in as good condition as any horse in the town. On the 26th of March he saw the horse in the defendant's field, in a horrible condition for want of food, there not being sufficient grass in the field to keep a rabbit alive. It died on the 27th of March. He had commenced proceedings in the County Court for dam- ages to the horse.—Mr. Dixon, M.R.C.V.S.' eleposed to • making apost mortem examination of the horse on the 27th ult., and said he considered death resulted from exhaustion through want of food.—Arthur Shawcross, M.R.C.V.S., said he made a po.it mortent examination on the 26th, and thought the horse had died from want of food and exposure.—lnspector Dowty having , given evidence, James Dainteth, publican' of Burton- wood, John Peek, John Kenwright, fa rmer, Burtonwood, gave testimony which was to the effect that there was abundance of grass in the field and that the animal though not in very good condition when Mr. Kelsall got it, was in an improving condition the dasebefore its death. Mr. Daieteth said on the night of that day the harse was lying in the field-file-and he and others tried to get it up but could not. They gave it a large quantity of, gruel, and bedded it well with straw and cloths.— Thomas Kelsall, son of the defendant, said he had, seen his father feed the horse well at various periods some weeks before its death. The defendant was fined 40s. and costs.

div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDLIN—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and Aldermen Harrison and Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERT.T.—Mary Kelly, in Foundry- St., on Saturday night, ss. and costs.-- John Gaskell, in Mill-lane. that night, 53. and costs.—Mary Ann Kenyon, on Friars' Green, the same night, sq. and costs.—Eliza- beth Ellen Fleming, in Scotland-road, that night, a' month's hard labour. As she was being taken out of the court by two constables she became excessively violent and assaulted them in court, screatnino. and swearing frantically. She was brought back, therefore, and sen- tenced to another morith's imprisonment. —Robert Baker, drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on Sunday night, Sc. DEE/NlL—John Gandy and Ann O'Dowd Were charged with being drunk in the New Market, on Saturday night. A constable fotind them sleeping on a stall. She had to be brought to the police station in a hand cart. They were fined ss. and costs each. WIFE ASSAULT.—WiIIiam Carey; labourer, 12, Carlisle- st., was charged under a warrant with assaulting his wife, but as his wife did not appear, haying forgiven him, he was let off with payment of costs. YIGHTING.—Annie McCone, fustian cutter, 4, Friar's- lane,and Margaret, Bonney, 11, Bucklev-st., were charged with fighting on Saturday night. On being separated by the police they pulled handfuls of hair out of each other's heads. McCone did not appear and a warrant was issued for her. Dnoney was bound over and had to pay Costs. PITCH AND Toss.—James Hardy, 11, Albert-st., John Barratt, 9, Refuge Square, Percy Cotterell, 7. Albert-st., lohn McKean ,14,Pierpoint-st „and Frederick Desborough, 10, Ed ward-st., all boys. over 14, for playing at pitch and toss on Sunday afterry,on, were fined Is. and costs . each.—Wm. Mather, 12, Stevenson-st., Abel Cliffe, 44, Naylor-st., James Ridgway, 3, Navlor-st ,John Wakefield, Naylov-st., and Thos. Moran, '29, James-at., all lads,

were charged with playing at football in ,Orford-st., on Sunday. The lads ran through people's front' t 0011 and out at the back to get away from the police. They were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs. . _

CHIMNEYS ON Roberts, School Brow, and James Daley, lodging-house keeper, Scotland-road, were fined is. each, for having their chmneys on fire. TUESHAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), and E. J. Guest. DRUNK AND DISOTDERLY.—Patrick 'Kilroy, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Friars Green, on Monday afternoon. The defendant's father said his son would not work, and was aged 30, and able to do for himself, but would not keep away from his house. He asked the mayor to make a "standing order" for the defendant to keep away. He was sent to prison for a month.—Thomas Henning in Horsentarket-Si., on Mon- day night, had a conviction recorded against him. SLEEPING OUT.—John Derbyshire and Wm. Kenwright were charged with being found sleeping that morning in the outbuildings of the Patten Arms Hotel. Derbyshire said he worked at the hotel, and they had to stop on the place overnight to meet passengers at the station.—Ken- wright said he was also employed at the hotel and slept there, and had to be on the premises at night in case of any orders coming.—The proprietor of the hotel did not appear against the men and they were discharged, en the understanding that they did not sleep in the out- buildings again without permission. WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Fairclough (chairman). and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. • ON ENCLOSED PREMISES FOR BAD A 'Johnson and Ellen Gibbing were charged with being found in Orford Barracks the previous night with intent to commit a felony. Sergeant Craythorne said he found the prisoners between the soldiers' quarters.—They said they had been lifted over the wall by three corporals.— They were bound over to keep the peace for six month. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—George Wheeler, for being drunk and disorderly in Stanley-st., the previous night, and assaulting his wife Margaret Wheeler, was fined 10s. and costs.—Thomas Caird, drunk and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st., on Tuesday night, was fined is. and costs. THErr or Boors.—William Jones,Ship Canal labourer; late of Manchester, living et the model lodging-house, was charged with stealing boots from the shop of Mr. G. Kirby (Public Benefit Boot Co., Braze-st.), and evi- dence having been heard in support of the charge, was fined 10s. and coqs, £1 9s. in all. UNSEEMLY BEHATIOUR.—EIiza Smith, for this conduct in Froghall-lane, on Tuesday night, was sent to gaol for two months. Tut:asp:ay.—Before Captain Rideavey (chairman) and Councillor James Fairclough: DRUNK.—John Swindles, drunk in* Scotland-road, the previous day, was fined Sc. including costs. Sciaat Casas.—At the instance of Mr. Geo. Riley, the following persons were dealt with for not sending their children to school :—Thomas Bradbury, 'labourer, Old- road, 53. Wm. Cartwright, forgeman, Tilley:street, 2:" Thomas Fernley, file cutter, Birchall-street, 4s. ThomA Fernclough, labourer, Helsby-street, order for the Clio.'] Wm. Keeley, factory hand, Hind-street, 2s. 6d. John Plunkett, labourer, Old-road, ss. Thos. Rowlinson, tan- ner, Latchford, 2s. J. Win. Wheeler, gardener, Latch- I ford, 5. FRlDAY.—Betore Aldermen Harrison (chairman) and Wright. • • WIFE DESElTlON.—Frederick Willitim Theinas, bar- man, last from Manchester, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Hoard of Guardians, with ab- sconding from Warrington on the 2nd inst., and leaving his wife chargeable to the Union. He promised to pro- vide her a home at Manchester.—The prikaier's aunt. of' Manchester, offered to provide a home for her.—The case': was adjourned a week, in order to allow the prisoner and, his aunt an opportunity of providing for her. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—John Percival. Park Side Farm; Preston Brook, was charged by Inspector Dowty,_ R.S.P.C.A., with cruelly treating a horse, by 'working it, while in an unfit state, at Warrington, on the 26th ult.: Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defence. Mr. Dowty gave: evidence that the horse, which had brought a load of potatoes that day to the market, was lame. There was a bony formation at the knee, and it was inflamed. The animal appeared to be in pain.—Mr. Jenkins said Mr. Dowtv, from his slender knowledge of the anatomy of a horse's knee, was unaware that a blow on any part of , the knee was liable to cause the formation he described; and it would cause the animal no pain.—alr.Bate, veteri- nary surgeon, stated that the formation would cause no pain. The animal was perfectly sound in every other respect.—By the Benet. : Thel. horse would not suffer pain if allowed to go slowly—at about six miles an hour. —The Chairman said that would not be slow.—The magistrates having vievred the horse in the street below,. fined the defendant ss. and costs. George Trenton, carter, Hall-st., Warrington, was charged by Inspector Dowty with cruelty to a horse, in Church-st., on the Ist Inst., by violently kicking it. P.C.'s Corbett and Berry and Mr. Dowty proved the case. The defendant was fined ss. and costs. _ _

A DELINQUENT APPRENTICE.—John and Joseph Wilkin- son, fustian cutters, Longford-st., summoned Catherine Carey, a child, their apprentice, for leaving her work, on the sth of March, putting them to an expense of Bs. —She was ordered to return to work, and pay the damages at the rate of ed. per week.

WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS. WEDbmsnAy.—Before Mr. John Rplands, Mr. W. H. Bleckly, and Major Pickmere. ASLHICP ON HIS Luura.—Thomas MaCDonald, for this offence at Sankey, on the 17th ult., was lined ss. includ-

ing costs. DRUNK AND DISORDHRLY.—Maria Simpson, at Sankey Bridges, on Tuesday evening, she having broken a win- dow, and caused a great disturbance because her hus- band had locked her out, was fined 103. and costs. DRUNK,—Edward Brown, for being drunk at Sankey Bridges, was fined Sc. and Costa. ASSAULT.—EIIen Hughes for assaulting Sarah Webb, at Sankey Bridges, on the 10th ult., was bound over to keep the peace.

WARRINGTON ROARD OF GUARDIANS: The fortnightly meeting of this Bonrd was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present Mes§rs, Rat- cliffe, Heaton, Shaw, Davies, D. Jones, Owen, War- burton, Diggle, Hood-Wright, Aukland, Harrison, Swinton, Jolley, Dobson, Humphreys, Smith, M- ahal], J. Houghton, Turton, Mather, W. Houghton. Dignum, Clarke, Hibbert, Rev. C. E. E. Carleton ; C. Sutton (clerk) and other officers.

div.head: ilia NEW GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR.
div.p: ilia NEW GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR.

A letter was read from Mr. Jenner Fust stating that he had been appointed government inspector for the poor-law district, in place of Mr. Henley, who has re- tired. He hoped soon to have the opportunity of mak- ing th 3 acquaintance of the Guardians. TIER LATE MR. RARMOURNH.

Mr.flanalsorr moved the following resolution, of which he had given notice :—" That, having regard to the fact of Mr. Harbourne's long and faithful services, and to the fact that his sudden departure harput an end to his chance of enjoying a superannuation allowance, and the fact that he has left a widow and a large family practically unprovided for, a gratuity of £5O, or such less sum as the Local Government Board may be pleased to sanction, be given to the widow." Mr. Harrison added that in Mr. Harbourne they had lost a very valu- able officer, and he sincerely hoped the resolution might be carried. Mr. Harbourne's wife and family were well entitled to any consideration which they could show them.—Mr. Devras secorided the proposal.—The CLEM( was afraid the question would arise as to the power of the Local Government Board and that Board to give a gratuity except for special services, but, as he should be in London shortly, he proposed to call on the Local Government Board and explain all the circumstances of the case to them.—This proposal was agreed to, and the ' motion was passed unanimously.

THH VALUER. A proposal that Mr. W. Owen be re-appointed valuer of the Union for the ensuing year, at a salary of £2OO, was agreed to. LIST OF ATTENDANCES. The Clerk submitted a list of attendances of the mem- bers of the Board during the past year. The total num- ber of attendances at Board and Committee meetings was as follows :—R. Kilshall, 32 : J. Humphries, 32 ; Thomas Smith, 59 ; W. Balharry, 55 ; J. Turton, 69 ; J. Swinton, 24 't D. Jones, 5 ; A. Jolley, 118 ; J. Clarke, 51; H. Hibbert, 57 ' • U. Ratcliffe, 102; R. H. Wright, 0 •' J. Dignum, 29 ; J. Houghton, 78; Rev. G. F. Roberts, 42 ; I J. Kilshaw, 9; R. Owen, 11; P. Warburton, 5 ; W. Houghton, 72 ; T. Mather, 26: E. Aukland, 69 ; a. I Blackhurst, 1 ; Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, 14; S. Davies,96 : W. Die.gle, 44 ; J Dobson, 61 ; W. Gill, 15 ; J. Harrison, 6 ; R. Heaton, 50; W. J. Shaw, 28.—The Clerk mentioned that Mr. Kilshall had been elected 27 years consecutively as a member of the Board for Burtonwood.—Mr. Harrison asked if Mr. Kilshall was his senior on the Board, and the Clerk replied that he was. He (the Clerk) had been connected with the Board longer than Mr. Harrison. and that was 26 years. Mr. Harrison would see that he was not; so old as he thought he was. (Laughter.) The Clerk added that both Mr. Diggle and Mr. Shaw had not been on the Board for the full twelve months. APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICER, &C. Part of the business before the Board was the appoint- ment of a relieving officer for No. 3 district, at a salary of £lOO. The applicants who had been selected to ap- pear before the Board meeting were :—Frank H. Auk- land, Froghall-lane, book-keeper ; Stephen H. Jenkine, Thelwall, missionary •, Frank Kerfoot,Bewsey Chambers, nuisance inspector; Frederick Wright,63, Padgate-lane ; and W.Wallace,Latchford,book-keeper. These applicants were separately called into the room, and asked various questions by the Guardians. A vote was afterwards taken which resulted in the appointment of Mr. Wallace, who, in the final vote,received 14 votes as compared with 11 for Mr. Kerfoot. -
A vote of thanks to the Chairman and vice-chairman for their service during the past year brought the meeting to a close.
