FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warringtpn, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. RUNCORN "A" v. Nnw BRIGHTON "A.".—The reserve teams of these noted Cheshire clubs met at Runcorn on Saturday, in grand weather. A goodly number of spec- tatms witnessed a capital game, in which the play shown was very interesting. In a one-sided contest, Runcorn won by four goals and four tries to New Brighton one try. WIDNBS A v. FRODSHAII.—The above teams met on the Widnes ground, on Saturday, in glorious weather. The game was of a give-and-take nature for some time, when the ball was rushed up by the visitors in a way that made the position look dangerous for the Widnes lads. Play was then centred in midfield, and nothing :occurred worthy of record. When half-time was called neither team had scored. In the second half, Play was very uninteresting. About five minutes before time the 1 isitors rushed the leather up the field, and it seemed as if they would score, but they were called back j They, however, secured a drop goal a moment after.. When the whistle sounded the visitors left the field .victors by 4% points to nil. WARRINGTON " A" v. LASCASTHR " A."—The weathis was quite summer-like in heat when theSe teams met a Lancaster. Warrington, who had, but,.a poor teatri,* started the game, and a splendid punt by Lawless sport I carried the warfare into the home 25. Here Rowe threw smartly to Lallyf who as smartly evaded his opponents, and ran over, but only a minor sias allowed. Flaying up in a most surprising fashion, the visiting forwards , screwed grandly, and sornb further passing between the half backs enabled Lawless • to kick finely, -Lancaster, i being decidedly lucky in eScaping with a minor. The I home team were then the aggressive party, but the I grandly judged kicks by Ashurat and ,IQalsiels carried the play to ita former positions:. Anotherautiful CORI- ' bined bitof work by the Warrington' forwards found itheletither being smartly passed, betsveerrf Laily,f Rowe;` Lawless, and Ashurst, and the last-named, swerving in, from touch,dropped it- grand goal. Taylor for the homes tars, then showed up with a dashing run, Leach forcing thti, game to the line. Taylor, Bailey, Higham, and Molyneaux tjuicklv relieved, and while the ball was bob-, hing about in thW-visitors'- half, Lally secured, and Made - a grand run -right to the line, Taylor scoring but again a minor was only allowed. A strong rash by Lancaster waS nullified by Lawless, and Daniels ran finely into his .opponents' 25. The Warringtonians were playing up splendidly; and after Taylor, Woods , Barnes, and Forster had Made a vigorous rush, ! Warburton dribbled prettily tithe line, where Hampson threw across to Lally, who ran in, for Ashurst to kick a beautiful goal. After this Taylor effected a fine piece of play, the result being a try to Atkinson's credit. Cross was then called upon, but he, in conjunction with Law- less, repulsed their opponents. A dangerous-looking rush was smartly saved by Ashurst, and being supplemented with a long punt by Taylor, the home quarters were again reached, and half-time arrived. Lancaster resumed the combat, but Lawless, Daniels, and Highs% drove them back to the line. A bout of passing by the visiting backs was then witnessed, and McPherson, in his endea- vour to clear, was run down by Bailey. Some fine kicking between Leach, Lawless, and Ashurst ensued, and another rush by the visiting forwards pressed the home team, the ball being passed out to Daniels who rushed over at the corner. After this, and while the game was raging in the home quarters, Lancaster broke away with a dribble to the visitors' 25, and a sharp move- ment enabled Leening to run in behind the posts, Taylor converting. Lancaster now pressed, until Lally effected a capital relief, and the visitors' forwards carried the ball to the posts. Again Lancaster broke clear away, and the ball being passed out to Taylor, the last-named gained a fine try. A couple of capital efforts by Taylor almost resulted in a try to Warrington, but although they pressed severely, nothing was scored, and Warrington won by 2-1-4 to 1-2-0.

exchanges between Plutnpton and Houghton took place, and after repeated attempts had been made tq cross the line, Hollingworth ran in and Hughes Converted the point. After a Sudden break away of the horns for- ward, Davies put in a sprint and scored a resulting goal by Hughes, and from this point th 3 , home lot were disorganised. Davies ran in a second try shortly afterwards, and Pendlebnry followed suit later on, bringing up the total to three goals and two tries to nil. Despite the absence .of suci players as Abrams, Faulkner, Riley, and Williams, Runcorn's combination was brilliant, especially during the second half, when the fast pace had a serious effect on the New Brighton men, and ,Runcorn had matters as they pleased: The visiting backs were frequently pressed, but on no single occasion could fault be found with the play, whether in defensive or attack. Steel, a second team man scored during the first half, and at the interval this point repre- sented the merits of the two teams. The ' second try scored by Davies was one of the features of the after- noon's play, and the popular Runcorn three-quarter received quite .an ovation for his clever performance. Houghton played his usual safe game, and his tackling repeatedly upset the calculations of the New Brighton men. Davie., and Pendlebury put in a vast ansount of work at three-quarters, and of the front 'division none did better than Massey, Steel, and Gayter.

County honours rest with Yorkshire, with Lancashire a very good second. It was only by a penalty kick that the championship passed from one shire to the other, and with the exception of this one failure Lancashire played up to their reputation. They have scarcely an clean a bill ef fare as twelve months ago, but for all that they have given much satisfaction.

It is when we come to club form that we find a fallieg away. None of the Lancashire teams have shown sueqb consistently good play as we were accustomed to a fes'i seasons back. If we examine the performances of the sixteen best clubs in Lancashire,Yorkshire, and Cheshire we And the first four places oceupied by representatives of the White -Rose', with Runcorri filling the fifth position. Warrington can'Show a better average than any of their Lancashire rivals', Swinton coining next, and;Wigan close up. ..Wigan have been somewhat erratic, a good full back and an extra three-quarter having been badly wanted. Salfrird,have been, up and down by turns, but the last few weeks have seen them in something like their old form. Manchester, too, have had a rather chequered caie'er, although therohave been occasions when they have done well. Neither of the two Bruragh;' , to clubs have cbvered themselves with glory. Oklhari. have now and again scored unlooked-fer•ltrjumphs, and they have one of the soundest defensive' 'divisions in the 1 county. , . f , Several of the Yorkshire teams have equated them- -olvadmirably. Both Leeds and -Br house Rangers have been wonderfully consistent, an they are well ahead of all riva's. The Rangers largely owe their posi- tion to their spleliaid—ffriiirds, than—wlionc there are none better in the shird. 'Miring thd earlier portion of the season Bradford liaß an unbroken list of suecesses ; but then the tide ;tuned, and disaster followed disaster with a regularity that took the gloss off their very fine record. It may be taken'as a sign of the times when we find one of the Southern Rugby counties establishing a cup competition in order to waken the waning interest in the garhe. That these competitions are popular is shown in the tremendous attendances at the ties in Yerkshire— there were 20,000 spectators at Leeds on Saturday,—but it by no means follows that they danduce tri the best football. There is a yearning for a Rugby League in certain quarters in Lancashire and Yorkshire. and few can doubt that such an organisation would give an im- mense impetus to the game. The very fact that a club would always be expected to turn out the very best possible team would be a guarantee of a good match; but the fact mush not be overlooked that this stipulation can only be rigidly enforced where players are paid for their services, and the founding 9f ayßugby Lytton would soon be followed up by a jirplanibfor the legalisa- tion of professionalism. 4 tn.., „me- a,
ASSOCIATION.

The magnificent victory of England at Ibrox Park, on Saturday, was a-fitting climax to a season which has furnished a great abundance of Association surprises. Who would have tipped West Bromwich Albion, for `instance, a very few weeks ago as the winners of the F. A. Cup? The "unexpected" has happened very often, , but everything was put into the ,shade bv the great match at Glasgow, So certain were the. Scottish authorities about success that the blow that fell on them in, the presence of a huge crowd of 25,000 en- thusiasts struck them with amazement: The Scotch team were not only beaten, but bsaten ignoininiously. WheniEdgar Chadwick opened the, scoring account in less than half a minute it was generally regarded as a flash in the pan. ~But it was only;e'prelude to a series of dazzling succesea, and when nig' end,foupd the Eng- lishmen conquerors by four goals to one the consterna- tion of their rivals was complete. For the first time since these international fixtures were started, 21 • years since, England have obtained two successive victo- ries. The end of the League tournament will^not be reached ' until the last Saturday in April, butlt maybe taken for granted that the top and bottom positions will be fillqd by Sunderland and Darwen respectively. The first- named have been very consistent in their League engage.' ments, and they look like carrying off the championship pretty easily. Although there is an ancient halo about the F.A Cup, everybody knows that it requires a good deal of luck to go right through the ties, and that it is a vastly different thing to win the League honours. The principle on which the League Cup is contested is the ' real test of merit, and the club that finishes up in the top position is undoubtedly the champion of the year. None of the Lancashire clubs have • followed up their successes of the past few seasons, the reason being that one and all require a plentiful supply of young blood.

The Alliance has proved very interesting owing to the close race between Notts Forest and Newton Heath. It is just on the cards that the Heathens may win the championship, but this can only be accomplished by the complete falling away of the Forest in the remaining fixtures.

Bury are certain to walk off with the Lancashire League championship for the second year in succession. They are vastly superior to all their rivals, their record being magnificent. Only once have they known defeat. They are in the semi-final for the Lancashire Cup, hav- ing to meet Everton at Deepdale to-day (Saturday), the Rovers and Darwen playing off their tie at Ewood Park the same afternoon.

div.head: WIDNES T. BARROW.
div.p: WIDNES T. BARROW.

Played at Barrow, on Saturday. Widnes kicked off and began to press. Chapman relieved. Dickinson ran and passed to Trewick, who kicked to touch at 12,1 f-way. The Widnes forwards dribbled to the line, Barber scoring but the place kick failed. After the drop out Widnes continued to press. A free kick from Barrow for offside play brought a relief run by Dickinson, and a dribble by Moore forced Foster to kick dead. After the drop out play settled in midfield, Haney kicking across the field to Dickinson, who ran to the 25, passed to Haney, the latter throwing forward. Widnes worked the ball to half.way, but Barrow were soon back again. From the line out Blezard got hold and scored behind the posts, the goal kick failing. Barrow continued to press. Dickinson scored a grand try. Parkinson kicked the goal. From good forward play Farmer scored for Widnes. The visitors pressed till half-time, when the score was : 1 Barrow 1 goal 1 try, Widnes 2 tries. During the second half Craig scored twice for Widnes, but near the close 'rrewick and Moore notched tries for Barrow, and goals being placed by Parkinson, the homesters won a grand game by 3 goals and a try to Widnes a gaal and three tries.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.

This return match took place at Leigh. on Tuesday evening, before a large " gate." Smith kicked off at 6.15, and some brilliant exchanges were witnessed in the first minute between Coop, Boscow, Webster, and alcMasters. When these operations had concluded play was at half way, and passing by Evan Anderton, and Pendlebury brought about an invasion of the Warrington quarters. The defence was sound, and Turner' in con- junction with Bate, checked the attack. Warrington now became the attacking party, by the aid of Antrobus, Bate, Jolley, and Webster, but Coop was in brilliant form, and the repeated endeavours of the visitors' for- wards were frustrated in a marvellous manner. Boscow and Coop again exchanged, but a smart run by Evan and ' pass to Anderton reached the visitors' quarter flag again. Bate ran finely down the open, and Coop was again reached ,but Anderton ran the oval back,only to see Ashton dribble back into neutral territory. Passing by Antro- bus, Bate, snd Jolley reached the Leigh line, and Webs- ter made his mark, the kick realising nothing. The game fluctuated considerably, and neither side could claim any distinct advantage. Warrington lost a grand oppor- tunity a moment later, when Coop was at fault, but an over-anxiety saw Anderton clear his lines and the oval taken to the Warrington goal. Jolley came away and punted over Coop's head, but the home custodian re- gained possession and danger was averted, this latter item bringing half time with not a point scored. The second half wa's of an unusually vigorous nature. In the first few minutes Webster was nearly in from a brilliant piece of play, but from this the tackling was of unusual severity, and the game was chiefly confined to the forwards. Two minors were credited to Leigh, and the final result consequently read as a draw. NEW BRIGHTON v. RUNCORN. Played at Liscard, on Saturday, before a good muster of spectators. The sides were not representative, Ing- ham and Hurst lending a hand to their neighbours, while several of the Runcornians' second team. figured in _ _ _ .
place of Crompton, Riley, Faulkner, Abrams, -and Wil- liams. A late start was made, and following the kick

fliTen ce on the home lin W, but only a minor point resulted. Dropping out, the Brightonians got well down, Pendlebuty making ineffectual efforts to break away. Jones put in some good work, nut was op- I posed to safe tackling, when Ingrain was tested, and the ball was sent into touch at the half-way line. Davies sped along the wing, but was well checked by Ingram, though for a long time the home line was hotly besieged. A free kick relieved some- what, and as Plumpton had arrived, and the team thus completed, it seemed that the homesters would certainly secure a point, for the line broke away in good style, and as Houghton was prevented from returning, matters looked ominous for the Run- cornians. Plumpton dashed along, but was met by Houghton, and shortly following, essayed at goal, but without effect. The forwards eventually gqt the oval away, and after a scramble in the home end, Steel rushed over and scored the first point for the visitors, Houghton's attempt at the place being a failure. After dropping out, the visitors again returned to the attack, but found Ingham in a tough mood, and nothing further was done in the way of scoring up to the interval. Massey restarted, and, following Plumpton's return,the home forwards made a determined rush to the Runcorn line, where Hughes saved finely, and cleared the danger. div.head: WARRINGTON,. LANCASTER.
div.p: WARRINGTON,. LANCASTER.

The return match between these clubs took place at Wilderspool, on Saturday, in weather which would have more suited the summer pastime of cricket. The mild- . ness of the weather naturally brought a lot of people out, but the large gate must be attributed to the fact that Warrington were beat on wiping out what they termed " the flukiest win recorded against them this season." The first match on January 2nd had resulted in a victory for Lancaster by a try, and all who witnessed that con- test referred to the amount of ill-luck which attehded the efforts of our local club. Each side had absentees, and it was 3.50 before a start was made by Fair Turner' kicking off towards the pavilion goal,-the oval finding touch near the Lancaster quarter flag. The visiters I screwed a scrimmage; and Potts saved daringly, but ome fluctuating play at centre eventually saw Bate dodg- ing in fine form, and causing Cowell and Bleasilale to fall back-and save their lines. Bles.sdale relieved with a tricky' run' ' and a moment later Turner struggled through gain- ing but a few yards. Cowell waa applauded ,for,• fins. kick, and a rush by Kitchen and Pinch changed the venue, but Potts arid Cowell exchanging kicks, • neutral grinind saw the battle being wageo.l,Fine passing by Antrobus, - Bate,' and Evans war succeeded by strong forward—Work' by Jolley and Thorniley, but , danger was averted when Kitchen and Dandy • came away with a clever dribble„ which reached Boscow, the latter finding touch. A peliaity, kick to VVarringten took play from their quarter flag ttl Lancaster territory, and another rush by Turner and Ashton ' ivas saved by Thompson. Bate tricked his opponents well and then Antrobus stole beautifully away, and passing to Webster the latter punted to Winder, and no response was forth- coming. Evans next received from Bate, and again Winder was tested, with no substantial result. , These successive failures of the Lancastrians led up to the homesters attacking. A neat display by Antrobus,Bate, and Potts, took play near the line, and after, the former had passed forward near the posts, Bate got the oval away from a scrimmage, and passing finely to Webster, the latter raced over near the corner. Turner took the difficult place kick and landed a fine goal. 'I horniley dribbled well on the re-start, • being checked by Thomp- son, but Boscow replied. The Lancaster forwards retaliated, and a fdoting was obtained in the Warrington quarter, Bate eventually dribbling through and reaching half-way, the liomesters headed by Turner, Beckley, and Donohue, again reached the Lancaster line,•l3l
leas- I

dale saving b'rillrantly, and from a pass by Bate, Webster tried a shot at goal, the oval falling short. Potts was within an ace of scoring the next minute, but Thompson got clear and reached half-way, where he fell into the safe clutches of Turner. Jolley next had a turn, but Bleasdale and. Garth relieved, whilst a piece of brilliant play by Potts saw the oval being „forced over the line, Ashton being a yard ' short in failing to register a substantial score. A minor fell to each side, and he* Lancaster' by the aid of the vigorous play of their forwards, and some judicious tackling by Thompson, and Winder, attacked.- Aparti- ality for Bate by Garth penalized the visitors again,and nozeply having been elected, Bate threw to Antrobus, who-ran and passed to Thorniley, the latter being grassed before he could make headway. Ashton was prominent with a clever mark, and although the game was taken near the Lancaster line, the visitors played up with renewed vigour, and Kitchen dribbling past Boscow, the latter fielded the oval, but in screwing for touch sent the Baal to Thompson, and the latter com- pleted the try, Bleasdale placing the sides ori 'equal terms with a neat goal. Half-time was called with each sides goal and a minor. Kitchen restarted, and Potts, Nevins, Bleasdale, and Boscow exchanged, the home- 1 sters having the best of matters. Bate and Antrobus passed neatly across the scrimmage, and another spell of exchange kicking between the custodians ended with advantage to Cowall. Bleasdale ran splendidly at this juncture of the game, and two runs of his were ap- plauded to the echo. Randles, Jolley, and Webster transferred operations to the visitors' 25, and although

the game was a trifle monotonous owing to the repeated scrimmages and rushes,the Lancaster men now began to show signs of distress. The Warrington team evidently had the measure of their opponents' and a dashing run by Potts was stayed by Winder. Webster next made his mark, and Turner had hard lines for the goal. Play was still confined to the Lancaster quarters, and Teare was once held under the poste. The oval was got away, but Jolley and Donohue returned to the attack, and Bate I had a shot at goal—a weak attempt. Fiva minutes from time the Warringtonians passed well, and Bate eventu- ally throwing to Webster, the latter scored near the corner. Turner failed at the difficult place. Following this came a sensational run by Bate on the stroke of thne,for, gathering the oval at centre field, he outwitted his opponents, and scored between the posts, Evans's failure at goal bringing time with the score—Warring- ton, 1-2-2; Lancaster, 1-0-1. div.head: SHIP CAPTAIN DROWNED AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: A SHIP CAPTAIN DROWNED AT WARRINGTON.

An inquest was held by Mr. F. A. Jones, the new deputy coroner, on Monday afternoon,in the Parade Room, Police Station, concerning the death of Frederick Furfy, aged 35 years, captain of the flat " Busy," belonging to the Manchester Ship Canal Co., who was drowned last night week, under the following circumstances :—Lydis Ann Fatly, wife of the deceased, deposed that she last saw him alive about a quarter past ten on Wednesday night, at home, 16, Eastham-st., Liverpool. He was not able to swim, but was a temperate man.—Edward Pres- cat, employed on board the" Busy," said he came in the flat with the deceased from Birkenhead,reach- ing Howley Quay, Warrington, about 3.30 on Friday afternoon. He left the boat between 7 and 8 at. night and had a walk round the town, and had two or three glasses of beer, and they were returning to the boat about 11 o'clock, the night being dark and foggy, when witness stayed behind, about 100 yards from the boat, leaving the deceased to walk on. He followed shortly after, but saw nothing of him. He heard no splash or. scream. Whea he got on board he could not find the deceased there; and the watchman George Mason, felt puree the boat with a he* to see if he could feel any- thing, but could not. Witness told Joseph Ellis in the morning. The deceased only had a couple of glasses of beer, but he being a stranger he thought the palice might have got hold of him and locked him up.—Ajury- man said the deceased was in his shop at 8 o'clock on the Friday night, perfectly sober.—Joseph Ellis deposed to the deceased's body being found not more than half-a- -dozen yards from the beat.—P.S. Taylor said he saw the deceased taken out of the water about a quarter to three on Saturday afternoon. He found in his pockets £1 75., a watch and gu,ard, and a pipe. The jury re- turned a verdict that the deceased was drowned through accidentally falling from the quay on the night of the Ist inst.

div.head: 4,IPALLEGED MURDER AT MANCHESTER.
div.p: 4,IP- ALLEGED MURDER AT MANCHESTER.

At Salford, on Monday, John Kelsall was charged with having burnt his wife to death. The evidence showed that Kelsall went home partially drunk on Satur- day,and without saying anything threw a lighted paraffin oil lamp at his wife. The lamp struck her on the fore- head, the glass chimney was smashed, and the burning oil spilled upon the woman's clothes. She was instantly enveloped in flames, and was subsequently found by a neighbour lying on the floor burnt to death. Prisoner was remanded.

div.head: A. WARRINGTON SLANDER CASE AT THE ASSIZES.
div.p: A. WARRINGTON SLANDER CASE AT THE ASSIZES.

At the Liverpool Aesizes on Saturday, George Howard, metal merchant, of Warrington, hula ght an action against Alfred Stirrup, to recover dam- ages for slander. Mr. Shee, Q.U., and Mr. Horridge were for the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulholland for the defendant, who keeps the Soldier's Return public- house in Warrington. According to the plaintiff's case opened by Mr. Shee,the parties were acquaintd with each other. On the 12th January they and several other men were in the Central Hotel billiard room, and an altercation took place as to whose turn it was "to have the table." The defendant turned to the plaintiff and said, You only drink lemonade and port wine to keep sober, so that you can rob people." The plaintiff would have taken no notice of that reflection on his character, but on the following night, when they were again in the billiard-room, the de- fendant, who was perfectly sober, said in the presence of several persons," I don't get my living by robbing peo- ple like him. He is a convicted thief. What about the copper and lead that he stole ? " That was the slander complained of. The only ground for the suggestion as to the copper was that some time ago the plaintiff's son was tried at Liverpool for receiving some metal knowing it to have been stolen. He was, however, honourably acquitted.—Several wit- nesses were called for the plaintiff, and they were cross- examined as to whether the plaintiff had not accused the defendant of making people drink to rob them.—Mr. Mulholland said the case was simply a pothouse squabble adjourned from a place of entertainment in Warrington to the Liverpool Assizes. He admitted that the defend- ant did say something nasty, but only when nasty things had been said about him.—The defendant said that on the second night a man said to him that he made people , drunk in his house to, rob them, adding, "You heard I Howard say that the other night." All that he (defend- I ant) replied was, "Well, I am not convicted of it; there is no copper or lead about our place." He never used the words that plaintiff was a convicted thief.—Several witnesses were called.—His Lordship said that as re- garded the language used on the first night, both parties seemed to have ended "quits." The question was whether that observation applied to the second night. It was a question which of the persons was most abused on the second night, and the jury must appraise the differ- ence.—The jury found for the plaintiff—damages £5; and his lordship gave judgment. These included a duet" The Venetian boat song," Mrs. Houston also sang " Entreat me not to leave thee" from" Ruth " and Miss Daly "Calvary." Mr. Walker Burlinson with his conjuring entertainment watt one of the other attractions in the course of the bazaar. The following are the names of the ladies who pre- sided at the stalls :—Alpha Stall : Mrs. Gunnell, Mra. Brough, Mrs. Entwistle, Mrs. Hardy, Mrs. F. Hardy,and Mrs. Hunt. Beta Stall: Mrs. and Miss Freeman, Mrs. Yonge, Mrs. Highley, Mrs. T. Brough, Mrs. Southern, Mrs. Gorst, and Mrs. Barlow. Gamma Stall: Mrs. Ross, Mrs. George, Mrs. Lawton, Mrs. Riddle, Mrs. Miles, and Mrs. Richards. Delta Stall : Mrs. Knowles, Mrs. Corradine, Mrs. Cotterill, Mrs. C. George, Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Atherton, and Mrs. Woods. Scholars' stall, Mrs. Walker. Refreshment stall, Mrs. John Bennett, and Mrs. Toft. Flower stall and fairy fountain, Miss Gornall and Miss Shaw-Green. The tea room was under the charge of Mrs. A. H. Dunn and Mrs. John Hayward, and the fishpond under that of Mr. C. George. Mr, C. Pritchard had charge of the curiosi- ties. The Rev. Thos. Ross acted as secretary in con- nection with the bazaar, Mr. Thos. Brough being assistant secretary, and the Rey. John Gunnell, the treasurer. The amount of the proceeds yesterday, and the .sum realised, are recorded in our local news columns.

div.head: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
FIXTURES FOR 1892.

By the list of matches arranged for the coming season by the secretary, Mr, C. H. Uusworth, War- rington have h most promising season before them. All the best clubs in the county are being met, day matches being arranged with Liverpool,Manchester, and Preston. The popular captain, Mr. S. M. Oros.- field, will again direct the first team, whilst the captaincy of the second team is entrusted to Mr. J. W. Parry,. Mr. W. H Robinson is the hon. _treasurer, and Mr. W. S. Howard assistant secretary and treasurer. Councillor R. 'l'. Fairclough is the president of the club; and the bowling green, which is a flourishing adjunct, is to be captained by Mr. Thomas Morris, Mr. George Pil- ling being secretary. The services of last year's profes- sionals, Fred Lee and All. Clark, are retained for the year I valuable acquisition to the membership of the club is the enrolment of Mr. A. C. MacClaren, the dell-known Lancashire County player, who, it is hoped, will be able to assist our local team when not engaged for the county. There are only two vacancies on the Warrington card, and it is expected that one, the 23rd July, will be filled up with a match against a representative county team, which Mr. Crosiield has promise I, if possible, to bring down. div.head: ALLEGED BIGAMT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED BIGAMT AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday, at Runcorn Police .Court, before Mr. 4G. L. Davies, Joseph Partiagton Ankers, aged 26 years, was brought up on a warrant, charged with feloniously marrying one Ann Edwards, his former wife Priscilla Ankers, being now alive. Inspector Cooper deposed that he took the prisoner into cus- tody at Wrexham. He made no reply to the charge. The inspector produced the marriage certificate of the second marriage, and he had compared it with the register at the registrar's office that morning.— Ann Edwards gave evidence that she married the prisoner at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Green- way-road. on the Bth April, 1888. The prisoner re- presented himself as a widwer.—Superintendent Atherton applied for s remand until Wednesday. 'Which was granted.

div.head: CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED SUICIDE
div.p: THE CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED SUICIDE
AT WARRINGTON

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, before Aldetrmen Harrison (chairman),Greenall (the Mayor) and Wright, the case of Alfred Hargreaves,labourer, 14,William-st.,adjourned from four weeks since,who stood charged with attempting to commit suicide, was called. He did not appear,but his wife was pre- sent, and said she had not seen him since 8 o'clock the previous morning. A warrant was issued against him, and he was brought up soon after. In reply to the Bench as to what he had been doing this week he said he had been drinking end working.—Alder- man Wright said he supposed it was drinking that bad put him out of his head.—Mr. Garnett,relieving officer, said the defendant was neglecting his wife, and she would have to come into the House soon if he did not look after her.—The defendant was about to join the militia, and he promised to try to amend. The case was adjourned for eight weeks.

ORT LINVIC R DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
ADOPTION OF AND SPEECH BY MR. BRUNNER, M.P.

The annual meeting of the General Council of the Northwich Division Liberal Association was held on Saturday afternoon, in the Gladstone Club, Northwich. There was a large attendance of mem- bers, no part of the division being unrepresented, and those present from Runcorn district included Messrs. E. W. Humphreys, W. Betney, T. Handley, J. Posnett, J. Clare, J. Withington, T. Lea, J. Lea, W. Carroll, T. Pickering, Boyle, A. R. Norman, G. Kirkham, T. Burrows, J. Taylor, J. Cooper, D. Bis- brown, and B. Crosby. Mr. H. Bratt, C.C., of North- wich, was voted to the chair.

TER RETORT. Mr. W. Handley (secretary of the Association) sub- mitted his annual report, which set forth that the pro- bability ot the election having to be fought on the pre- sent register caused their agents to give anxious attention to its preparation, and a great amount of preliminary work was done, and the information gathered, as the re- sult of surveys and local knowledge, was utilized so that the first lists of occupation electors might be as nearly correct as possible. As the result proved, they had not a great number of claims or objections to make on the occupation list,the work of that description being mainly on the ownership portion of the register,and they thought it would be found that very few indeed of those quali- hed would have been omitted, but that.
IN HARMONY WITH THE FRANCHISH ACTS,.

all, entitled by their yet cumbrous and prohibitive limitations, would be able to exercise their privilege. The number of electors on the register (including dupli- cate registrations) was 12,832,an increase over last year of .304, being the largest register in the county Cheshire. The special committee urged that a determined effort should be made to obtain a sufficient number of sub- scribers, so that the mind of their Treasurer might be eased, and the credit of the association maintained. At one time a contist seemed doubtfula not an improbable contingency, which would have been deplored both by their member and their constituency; but that state of uncertainty no longer existed, and, in Mr. George Whiteley, the Tory party thought they had a candidate who would excite the enthusiasm of the constituency, and possibly win the seat by converting and convincing what he had described as the" Foggy party," "a party of political parrots," and a" section of political macaws." (Laughter.) And quoting the well worn simile of the seemingly unequal

- - CONTEST BETWEEN DAVID AND GOLIATH. Mr. Whiteley had modestly suggested tnat Mr. Brun- ner might one day find that this David" by the sling of free speech and argument, and the stones of patriotism and common sense, had stricken him down from the high position he now occupied, and cut off his political head with his awn political speeches." It would, how- ever' be unwise and suicidal for them to underrate the forces arrayed against them, or the ardnuor and tenacity with which their position would be assailed and the codtest fought. (Hear, hear.) The danger of abstention must be clearly pointed out for, as often proved. Conservative success was usually the result of a small poll, and Liberal victory almost invariably followed the fullest expression of the voting power of the electorate. Every man should work, as if on him alone hung the issue of the day, from early morn to set of sun. In Mr. Brunner they had a candidate of large experience,

TILDID, TRUSTED. AND DETOTZD to his work, who had not yet been found wanting, and who was, on all hands, acknowledged to have done yeo- man and unselfish service for their constituency, no less than for the great Liberal party. In Mr. Gladstone they had s veteran leader, the wonder and admiration of the world, and to have fought under his banner, and that of those who so loyally supported him, was an honour which they and those who followed them might well be proud of. In the cause of Home Rule for Ireland they were privileged to have a noble part. (Applause.) The report was adopted on the motion of the Chair- man.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS.

On the proposition of Mr. E. W. Humphreys, the fol- lowing officers were re-elected:—Mr. E. H. Moss, J.P., president; Mr. G. 11. Deakin, chairman of council; Mr. H. Brett, C.C., chairman of executive; Mr. E. Milner, J.P. , C.C., treasurer; and Mr. A. Fletcher, hon. secretary . Twelve co-optative members of the council were also elected. _ .

Mr. A. Fletcher moved that the following gentlemen represent the Association on the National Liberal Federa- tion : Messrs. E. H. Moss, G. F. Brunner, C.C., A. R. Norman, P. Speakman, C.C., A. Fletcher, H. Bratt, C.C., E. Milner, C.C., H. Capes, Rev. F. Carter, J. Millington, J. M. Fell, T. Handley, and the Secretary (Mr. W. Handley). In moving the resolution Mr. Fletcher said he had included in the list the name of Mr. Speakman. They had received from

MR. M.S./114LN • letter which had caused the members of the Association very considerable regret. It was an intimation that he wished to withdraw from the Association. It seemed there had been a little friction at Runcorn of a personal character, which had excited the indignation of Mr. Speakman. He moved that the Council express its de- sire that he would re-consider the letter he had sent, and not insist on withdrawing from them. He had known Mr. Speakman for a good number of years and he could bear testimony to the fact that he had been • GOOD, SOUND LIBIGAL, FOR 30 'SNAGS, and had worked with them, and it would be very disas- trous if on the eve of an election one of their leading men should not give his full and cordial co-operation. He, therefore, should like an expression to go forth that they regarded him as

• 000 D BLICITHIIII 11l ABM, and that they hoped he would stick to them and they would stick to him. (Applause.) Mr. A. R. Norman seconded the resolution, and said he could bear out what Mr. Fletcher had said. The motion was carried unanimously. The President, the Secretary, and Mr. E. W. Humphreys, were appointed representatives on the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council.
TUB FINANCIAL STITHIONT was taken as read and adopted as satisfactory on the motion of the Chairman. ADOPTION OF MR. BRUNNBR.

The Chairman, in accordance with the recommendation of the Executive Committee, then moved that Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. be the candidate of the Association at the forthcoming General Election. (Applause.) Mr. Blagg (Winsford) seconded the motion, Mr. T. Handley sdpported the motion. He said in Mr. Brunnet they had a thorough Liberal, who was au fait with all question of a democratic or thoroughly Liberal character; and he had endeavoured to make himself master of all questions that had come before Parliament. He thought he might SPEAR OF RUNCORN _

and say that they -;.--e7; -r-ea.--di and full of fight—(ap. plause) ; they were prepared to put their shoulder to the wheel and if all the districts would do the same, they would return Mr. Brunner with a still increased majority. (Applause.) Mr. A. R. Nor man said there seemed to be a feeling that they in Runcorn were in rather a weaker position, but when they came to the Parliamentary election they would net be found wanting. (Applause.) The resolu- tion was carried with great enthusiasm, cheer after cheer being raised. Mr. Brunner was then called into the room, and the audience spontaneously rose to their feet and cheered vociferously. Mr. Brunner said he did not think he need tell them how delighted he was to have such a cordial reception front them. The sounds he had beard during the last few months seemed to him to be absolute proof that they were not only unanimous in their choice but absolutely -BPOZLINO YOU • FIORT.

(Laughter.) They knew that on several public occasions lately he had welcomed a contest in Northwich because, as a disciple of John Bright, he was convinced that an uncontested election was anlopportunity lost, and he welcomed a•contest because it gave to the can- didate an opportunity of making the acquaintance of of many men whom otherwise he would not know and of learning in a pCesaant fashion the desires and aspira- tions and hopes of the men whom he wished to repre- sent in Parliament. ,(Rear, bear.) There had been very few occasions, there were very few subjects, upon which he found himself at any difference with the Liberals of Northwich Division. (Applause.) Those who had followed his record with the House of Com- mons had never had to complain about a vote of his. (Hear, hear.) The nest Parliament would be not only a Home Rule Parliament bat

A PARLIAMENT OP ROCIAL WORM. (Applause.) Amongst social reforms was one which had given him more painful thought than any other political question with which he had to deal ; he meant reform of the Poor Law. Men had came to him time after time with their mind full of soreness and a certain feeling of injustice that a man who had paid rates all his life was not entitled by law to relief at the hands of the public ; that if he obtained it, those of his family who were able to pay, were compelled to contribute towards his sup- port. After all the thought he bad given to it, he did not think it would be right to relieve sons who were able to pay from the charge for the support of their parents. His first reason was that if they declared by law that a son ought not to support his parents, they, as far as the law could do, destroyed filial affection and they went direct in the teeth of the old commandment " Honour thy father and mother." (Applause.) But lie had always recognised that it wag absolutely wrong to treat deserving old people in the harsh and cruel fashion in which they did treat them at the present time. (Applause.) To compel decent respectable peo- ple to herd in workhouses with the vile and filthy people that they met there was

et CRIME AGAINST HUMANITY. ,(Ilear. 4ear.) Te his mind this could be amended by ' the ratePaYers taking care that on Boards of Guardians thereshould be a full and fair representation of the poor as arell as the rich. (Hear. hear.) If they abolished the property qualification for Boards of Guardians. as they had done for the House of Commons and the gckuntg Cpupcjj, they weak' get upon the Bctattl

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL

Guardians working-men themselves,and then they migh depend upon it that the poor would be treated with greater consideration than they were were now. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to his opponent, Mr. Geo. Whiteley, Mr. Brunner said the moment he came into the division he was received with open arms by the Conservative party ; they were absolutely at their wits' end to find a candidate, and the rankest outsider would be satisfac- tory to them. Be saw that they had chosen Mr. Hornby Lewis as president of the Conservative Association, another rank outsider, which showed to his mind that

THE STEADY-GOING CONSERVATIVE of Northwich Division was not entirely satisfied with the candidature of Mr. George Whiteley. There he had coma and there they had to deal with him; of this he felt satisfied, that Mr. Whiteley was going to behave himself as a gentleman, and they would behave like gentlemen too. They would fight him and fight him as hard as any man ever was fought. (Applause.) But he , was perfectly satisfied that neither Mr. Whiteley would hit below the belt nor that he (Mr. Brunner) nor anybody amongst the Liberal party would do that. Not long ago speaking at a licensed victuallers' dinner at Blackpool, Mr. Whiteley declared that he was coming to Northwich to DEFEND THE INTERESTS OF THE TRADE. They would remember the words he (Mr. Brunner) spoke from Mr. Thomas's shop in the Bull Ring at midnight on the first December, 1885—(applause)—when he congrat• ulated the men of Northwich Division that they had de- dined to vote for a man on account of his trade. He was sure that the men of Northwich Division were of the same mind that day; that they would this time not elect a man on account of his trade. In a recent speech Mr. Whiteley put aside his connection vritk the liquor trade, but they might depend upon it that it was because of his intimate connection with the liquor trade that he was there at all. (Applause.) Having alluded to Home Rule Mr. Brunner went on to say that the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council had drawn up a scheme of re- form somewhat wider in one or two points than the pro- gramme drawn up at Newcastle. He had been dissatisfied with the way in winch the programme of the National ' Liberal Federation had been arrived at, and be wished them to discuss thescheme of the Cheshire Association in every polling district in the division. There was net • word said about a

vantage of hearing upon the platform had been detained in London upon his Parliamentary duties. He did not think that ;that meeting could be described as a " lane chamber." It was anything but a "lone chamber," and he was happy to say it was only of a piece with all the other meetings which he had up to that time since the commencement of his candidature. (Hear. hear.) It had been a. great pleasure to him to meet so many of the electors of the constituency and their friends; it enabled-him to have ocular demonstration, if demonstration were necessary, that that was a working- man's constituency, and that the questions which inter- ested that constituency and that were important and vital to the constituency were working-men's questions. (Hear, hear.) Those were the questions with which the minds of the statesmen of the present day were mainly occupied. If they glanced over what he might call the ' recognised and authorised programme of the Liberal party they could have no doubt about that. Take them one by one, and they would see that they were either questions in which working-men were exclusively inter- ested or questions in which working-men had a direct and immediate interest, although they might also have an interest for large classes of the community who were not working-men. Allotments, employers liability, factory legislation, the housing of the working classes, ground rents, mining royalties and way-leaves—(hear, hear)—one man one vote—(hear, hear)—and the amend ment of registration law all those werequestions in which as he said before, the workingman had either an exclu- sive or a most immediate and vital interest, and those were the questions which would have to be determined in the Parliament which must be elected in the course of a very few months, and possibly of a very few weeks. .(Hear, hear.) Therefore, the coming election was, for the working-men of the United Kingdom, the most im- portant election that had taken place or would take place in the present century. It, therefore, behoved working-men to act wisely and well in the choice of their representatives. They had now a golden oppor- tunity. They had the power in their own hands, and it rested with them whether they would make good use of that power or not. Theluestion for them was,would they trust themselves to the Tories or would they trust themselves to the great Liberal party. The Tories were telling them that they were their friends, that they had been their friends in the past, and that, therefore, they might expect them to be their friends in the future ; and the Tories had been deluging that coastituency,as he be- lieved they had been deluging other constituencies, with handbills and leaflets, the burden of which was that the Tory was the workingman's friend. Let them consider that for a moment. Let them con- sider which of the advantages and liberties , the working-men at the present day possessed had been obtained for them by the Tory party and Liberal party. They had got a;cheap loaf. ((Applause.) That was a thing that came to him and to all of them. It came to him as the father of a family that possessed healthy appetites. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He was very fond of • cheap loaf, but was it the Tories who gave it them? ("No.") Why, the Tories were interested in • dear loaf, because dear bread and dear corn spelt high rents, and the Tory party were the party of the great landowners and all that depended on the great landowners. (Hear. hear.) Even yet they were not cured of their protec- tionist notions, for they were always talking of a thing called Fair Trade, and Mr. Chaplin was looking back with regret to the times when corn was at a much higher price than at the present day. (Hear, hear.) Was it the Tory patty who gave them the cheap newspaper P They resulted every attempt to emancipate the press under which it was formerly groaning. Was it the Tories who gave them the franchise? They never admitted anybody into the constitution outside the charmed circle of the classes that they could exclude. (Hear, hear.) They had got placed in their hands a great power which was absolutely essential for their protection, and that was the power of combination. To whom did they owe that? Was it to the Tory party? From the beginning of this century the Tory party had been the persistent opponents of placing that weapon in the hands of the working classes. It was not till 1871, when Mr. Glad- ston introduced his bill legalising trades unions and put- ting them upon a proper footing, that the working classes obtained that most essential means of protection. (Hear, hear, and applause.) And so he might extend the list if time permitted, but he had given them illus.. trations enough of the degree to which the working classes were indebted to the great Liberal party for the advantages and liberties which they at the present time enjoyed. (Applause.) Be wanted them to consider what was the particular Government in power when a' particular measure was passed for the benefit of the' working classes. They must consider what was the party that originated that measure, what was the party that fought for it, and what was the party that opposedl it until all opposition was hopeless. (Hear, ,hear.) It was difficult to retain one's patience when one read in the newspapers and in those pamphlets and leaflets the self-glorification of the Tories over the so- called Liberal measures, which they passed for the benefit of the workingmen. (Hear, hear.) He thought there was hardly any parallel for it except something which he noticed occurring from the newspapers. A gentleman, and, curious to say, a very important func- tionary of the law who had resigned his place, had taken to lecturing in favour of the abolition of capital punish- ment. (Laughter.) Mr. Berry upon such a platform as that was not a more extraordinary spectacle than the Tory party congratulating themselves and taking credit to themselves for passing such a measure as, for instance, free education. (Hear, hear and ap- plause.) Were the working men of England going to be befooled by the Tories? If they were he could only say they deserved to be befooled, and they would have nobody but themselves to blame. (Hear hear.) As he had said before they had now a golden opportunity. The time was fast approaching when at the poll they would be enabled to show to the Tories that they were not to be caught with chaff, and that when the Tories posed as the friends of the working elassses the working classes were sufficiently intelligent and clear-sighted to see through the device and the sham. The workingmen of Warrington would not, he thought, be behindhand in reading that important lesson to the Tory and Unionist party. (Loud applause.) Miss Daly then gave a song in a style which won the enthusiastic appreciation of the audience, by whom she was warmly encored. Mr. J. T. TAYLOit expressed the pleasure he felt in speaking on behalf a man whom lie respected so highly as he did his friend Dr. Houston. They had heard that night from Dr. Houston a speech which showed to them not only his attachment to Liberal principles but also a subtlety and intellectual power which was certainly rare in this generation. (Hear, hear.) Dr. Houston was a curious example of Lord Salisbury's Hottentot. (Laugh- ter and loud applause.) He imagined that if Lord Salis- bury or his cynical nephew were to look over the back benches of their fox-hunting followers they would find that it would need twenty years of resolute instruction before they would be fit to be compared with Dr. Hous- ton. (Applause.) Dr. Huston was a man who in darker days than these, was a Radical and a Home Ruler as he was to-day, and at a time when character was tested and men's consistency was really brought to the proof Dr. Houston was to be found then as he is now. (Loud applause.) He thought it as well to say that, although he could see that Dr. Houston had won the confideu cc of the people of Warrington, but stills word from a man's neighbour was the best test that could be given of his character. He would say this to them, that their honour and their political represen- tation were safe in Dr. Houston's hands. (Loud applause.) Dealing with the Irish question Mr. Taylor said the real Radicals were all at the present time arrayed behind Mr. Gladstone in the great policy of justice to Ireland. (Applause.) What the Irish people asked was simply that they should have extended to them the same system of government which had been extended with such salu- tary effect to Canada and Australia. When that fight was over and when they had sent an able, a worthy and a consistent Radical and Home Ruler to represent them in Parliament, and when the great issue of justice to Ireland was brought forward in Dr. Houston. Warring- ton would speak with no uncertain voice. (Hear, hear!, and loud applause.) Councillor Fonanto moved, and Mr. W. PIERPOIXT seconded, a vote of thanks to the speakers and singers, and this having been cordially passed, . Mr. Leach= responded, and the meeting then terminated.

RECEPTION LAST EVENING. Last evening the Working Men's Mission at Bank Quay, was crowded with an enthusiastic audience. Mr. A. 11. Crosfield presided, and amongst those present were Dr. and Mrs. Houston, Mr. R. H. Todd, L.L.D., Dr. Markel, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Councillor J. H. Fleming, Mr. C. J. Holmes, Councillor S. Green, Dr. Gornall, Councillor H. Roberts, Mr. H. Bond, Mrs. W. Pierpoint, Miss Pierpeint. Miss Fleming, Mrs. F. Loughlin, and Miss Cavanagh. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with loud applause, said there was a political part and a musical part of their programme, and he was very glad that they should be able again to draw upon the services which had been so readily accorded at their previous meetings of the gifted lady who had done so much by her activity and example to help to generite and to extend that common spirit which was produced by working for a common and a good purpose, a spirit which would be no unimportant factor in the victory which they hoped to be able to achieve. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had beard from one or two of their Tory friends a little good-humoured criticism at the introduction of music into those political meetings. But if the ancient Greeks made music and gymnastics the basis of their .education he did not see why they should not accept music in politics—(hear, hear)—and as their Tory friends had so great a respect —he might say an inordinate respect, for antiquity, he did not think they ought to take exception to what they called this new departure. (Hear, heae.) The question now was to which party and to which member they were to confide their interest. If experience was to count for anything he thought the Liberals had a strong claim upon their support. The Liberals could not claim to have passed every one of the measures which had benefitted their country in the last 50 years, but even when they had not passed them he thought that, as a rule, they had brought a little pressure to bear, a little of the pressure that was necessary to induce the Tory party to take the

step that was wanted. They had contributed by the process admirably and succinctly described the other day by Mr. Courtney as "prodding." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Dealing with the Irish question, Mr. Cros- field said he believed a certain amount of capital was made, and improperly made, out of the old religious question, the old "no Popery" cry. (Hear, hear). All he wanted to ask was,if,upon the granting of Home Rule the Catholics would proceed to oppress their Protestant neighbours, how was it that so many of the most able and acute leaders of the Irish in their agitation for Home Rule had been Protestants. (Hear, hear). Was it likely that these men would commit either political or social suicide? ([leer, hear). And, secondly, why, when the Protestants alone formed the Irish Parliament from 1780 to 1800, they had practically made up their mind if the Parliament had lasted to admit Roman Catholic members. (Hear, hear.) Besides, supposing it was decided not to grant Home Rule, what did their Tory friends inteadto do with the 80 Nationalists? Did they propose to convert them or to "sack" them. (Hear,hear.) It was said that they were not agreed to all the clauses which would form the Home Rule Bill, but they were satisfied to leave a certain amount of latitude as to the details, and even the important details of Home Rule, to the master-min, the great specialist, who of all men they knew was the mos t competent to deal with it. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) A song was then given by Mrs. Houston, and she was warmly encored. Dr. Houston then rose amidstenthusiastic applause. He said from what he knew of the Warrington people he 'felt it he stood there simply as an Irishman who had experienced the sorrows and sufferings and shared the hopes of his country and asked them on that ground and for her sake with love to help them to get back that legislature of which they were basely robbed—(ap- plause)—he should meet with a generous and Sympathe- tic response. And he was quite sure the people of 1 Warrington would not be frighteaed of the people of I Ireland demanding foolishly and insanely to be separated ! from England. (Applause.) Be did not think the I Irish would be so foolish as to be anxious to ' establish a separate state with a Tory fleet and the burlesque of an army, and ambassadors at the court of the Mikado, and the Sultan of Timbuctio— (laughter)—that his Catholic fellow-countrymen enter- tained the infamous and nefarious design of plundering and oppressing their Protestant fellow-countrymen. (Applause.) He thought he should succeed in Warring- ton on that plea alone. But that plea was fortified and sustained by another, addressed to this country's sym- pathies, to its vital and immediate interests, because until this eternal Irish question was disposed of the grie- vances of the people of England would never be redressed. The only way the difficulties could be surmounted would be by turning out Lord Salisbury and putting in Mr. Gladstone. (Loud applause.) They had been threatened with the House of Lords. Some time or otber they would have to deal with the House of Lords—(L Voice: The sooner the better)— and as one of the audience said the sooner perhaps the better. He was not an advocate of raw haste, the half-sister of delay, and if the House of Lords could be brought into touch and sympathy with the people and made useful to the country, he would not the one for destroying it. (Applause.) The doctor Qom- wonted on the slowness of procedure of the House of Lords and the small amount of time they devoted to the business of the country,and he humorously remarked that there was one body of men at all events that did not require an Eight Hours Bill and that was the House of Lords. (Laughter.) If that House were not prepared to pass a well-consideredlmeasure that was demanded by the people then it might be worse for the House of Lords If Coercion Act or smoother Act that was not desired by the people was to be passed, the wheels were allowed to revolve as quickly as they could. Dr. Houston next dealt with the subject of the housing of the working. classes and referred to the condition of things in this respect as disclosed by the report of the commission of 1884—a state of things which was perfectly appalling. It showed indeed that in many places in London 7, 8,10 and 12 people were living in a single room, This sort of thing existed not only in large centres of population but also in the rural districts, where there could not be the smallest shadow of excuse or extenuation for it. I Considering that the working classes were prevented s , number of days in the year from working, through ex- ' haustion caused by living in such houses it was the one burning question that ought to be pushed quickly for- warned if they wanted to save the lives of the people. (Applause.) Dr. Houston said no doubt the Tories were taking credit for the Bill for the housing of the working classes passed in 1890, but he characterised it as a sham; and said the only way to get the problem solved was to turn out the present pretenders who oc- cupied the treasury bench, and put a man into their place. (Applause.) After s song, and an encore, by Miss Cavanagh, Dr. TODD, of Londonderry, then addressed the meet- ing. He denied the claim of the Tories to the credit of having governed Ireland well, and said the Light Rail- ways Bill and Land Purchase Bills had been of no rea advantage to the country, because thay had been ad- minitsered in the interests of an oligarchic clique.; After some more musical entertainment of the audience, the proceedings concluded with votes of thanks to the I lady singers, Miss Fleming, the pianist, and Mr. H. Bond, violoncello.

It is is obvious that the preparation of these remark- ably successful Receptions has involved no small amount of labour and supervision. The Finance Committee, who have them in hand,are Mr. W. Pierpoint (chairman) Councillor H. Roberts (hon. sec.), Mr. J. C. Holmes (hon. treasurer), Councillor Fleming and Dr. Gomall. They have been assisted,of course, by Mr. John Clayton, Liberal agent, and every credit is deserved for the ad- mirable manner in which the arrangements have been carried out.
MORE RECEPTIONS.-MASS MEETING.

To-night a reception will be held at the Temper- ance Mission Room, Latchford; on Monduy there will be a reception.at Brick-street Schoolroom, and on Thursday evening at the National Schools, Church-strest. On Wednesday evening a mass meeting of Liberals will be held in the Public Hall, Rylands street, when addresses will be given by the Right Hon. Samuel Walker, Q.C., (Irish Attorney- General during Mr. Gladstone's last administration), Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., Dr. Houston, Q.C., and others.

He was not an enemy of; sport, but he liked a man who pursued game to have some exercise When he went for his sport—if so be it, there were some element of dangerte his own skin—but when pheasants were bred and fed like barn door fewls and driven by hundreds and thousands into corners for him to shoot with guns loaded for hina by a man behind, he called this not fair sport but

div.head: LIBERAL RECEPTIONS AT WARRINGTON
div.p: LIBERAL RECEPTIONS AT WARRINGTON
THERSDAY.-IN THEICO-OPERATIVE HALL:.

The reception of Thursday evening was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st.. and there was again a crowded and enthusiastic attendance. Mr. C. J. Holmes presided, and amongst others present were Dr. Houston, Q.C., and Mrs. Houston, Miss Daly, Misses De Deere, Mrs.. Fleming, Mrs. Pierpoint, Mrs. A. Browne, Mrs, H. Roberts, Mrs. Loughlin; Mr. I. Leadam (Liberal candi- date for the Altrincham division), Mr. J. T. Taylor. Barrister-at-Law, Mr. J. Ryland, J.P., Dr. Gornall,J.P., Mr. W. Pierpoint, Councillor J. H. Pleming, ,Councillor H. Roberts, Councillor A. Browne, Err. T. Birchall, Mr. T. Morris, &c. The 011111111 AN said they were at present living in stir- ring times in Warrington. After a period of rest and of political inactivity they had atlast aroused themselves to such a spirit of enthusiasm as had rarely been witnessed 'in the borough before. (Hear, hear.) Now, why did that spirit of enthusiasm so pervade every member of the party, from their venerable president, Mr. Rylauds, to the most humble member of the party? He thought the answer was not far to seek. They were all so certain that they had in Dr. Houston—(applause)--- an excellent candidate, a gentleman in whom they had the highest confidence, and a gentleman who if elected as their representative would do honour to the good old town of Warrington. (Applause.) The chairman of their Association had no apology to make for the candidate which the general Council had introduced to the electorate of the borough, and that was rather a different state of things to what existed at the Conservative meeting when the Chairman of that Association presided. The great objection which seemed to exist against Dr. Houston in the minds of some people was that he was a "foreigner." (Laughter.) That subject had been dealt with so ably by Dr. Houston and several other speakers that, perhaps, it seemed hardly necessary to him to allude to it in the least. He should, however, just like to take that opporunity of saying that he rather liked " foreigners," especially when they came from no further abroad than Ireland. It had been his good fortune to spend a considerable thaw in Ireland, and he could assure them, that, while he resided in that beautiful country, he received nothing but the greatest kindness in all parts, and, if there was any difference at all, he was received with the greatest cordiality in those parts where Home Rule ideas were practically unanimous. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Them was a little circumstance which was mentioned to him by a gentleman a few days ago, and it was a ratheruurions coincidence. Some of them might know --the ladies at all events would be aware of the fact— that the present year was leap year. (L tughter.) It was leap year when they returned for Warrington the late Peter alylands, and it was leap year when they returned their lamented friend, John Gordon McMinnies. It was now leap year, and it would be leap year when they re- turned their excellent candidate,Arthur Houston. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) They must make up their minds-that, at the coming election, they should work in such a way as they had never worked since that memor- able year when they returned their late friend, Mr. McMinnies, and victory would be theirs. (Applause.) A duet, entitled "My heart's delight," was then sung by Mrs. Houston and Miss Daly in a style which won a hearty encore, upon which they repeated part of the song. Mr. I. UMW!, the Liberal candidate for the Altrine- ham division.next addressed the meeting. He remarked that he regarded it as a signal honour to be invited to speak on behalf of such a candidate as theirs was. Of Dr. Houston's antecedents and great position he need not say anything, as by that time they were familiar to them all, but there was one point upon which he might be permitted to insist. In that election Warrington had a Special chance. There were not many constituencies in England which would have the opportunity of returning to the House of Commons a. bona-fide Home Rule Protest- ant Irishman. The great question for debate when the new Parliament meets, which he apprehended would be before many months had elapsed, would be the Irish question, the interminable, ever-present, and never-to- be-got-rid-of Irish question. Parliament would listen to those men who were qualified to speak with authority on that question, and there was no man at present out of Parliament who had more authority to speak than their friend Dr. Houston. (Hear, hear.) The voice of Warrington, so long silent, would again be heard in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) When it was heard it would carry with it the weight that it deserved. If he were to use commercial phraseo- logy he should say that Dr. Houston was an exceptional bargain to be secured at any cost. (Applause and laughter.) He spoke of the voice of Warrington and there was an echo to his words. There was more than one vacant seat in the House of Commons. There were two side by side. One was Warrington and the other was Altrincham. (Hear, hear, and laugh- ter.) They had been vacant practically for six years past. Dr. Houston could fill one, and he (Mr. Leadam) flattered himself that he knew who could fill, the other. (Laughter and applause.) There was at the present time a general sense of dissatisfaction with the Government, and the Tory party could rot think why they were so unpopular. There was, how- ever, always one interest before the eyes of the Tory party and that was the landlord interest. It was in fact the sacred ark of the Conservative covenant. Da was for the landlords that the Irish Coercion Act wadi passed and it was for the landlords that the Irish land I purchase acts were passed. (Hear, hear.) When he thought of Conservative pledges he was reminded of a well-known advertisement " the patent reversibles." A Conservative pledge was a patent reversible for they were sure to act diametrically opposite to what they had promised, and no more irrefutable proof of that could be found than those Irish coercion acts and land purchase acts. (Hear, hear, and applause.) At the present time the Conservative party were bringing forward a series of electioneering measures. They were not meant to work; they were to real measures what wax works were to real men and women, and he doubted very much whether they would be as effective with the electorate as the Conservative ministers fancied they would be. (Applause.) they were measures upon which the Con- slrvative party had spent years of denunciation and they were now only wrung from the Tory party when it was at its last extremity and were not likely to win popes-

lar gratitude. (Loud applause.) Mrs. Houston then gave a song in her usual admirable style, and in response to an encore she gave the song which is always popular with her audienees, entitled "What Paddy gave the drum." Dr. Housrox, on rising to speak, was received with acclamation. He mentioned that the Right Hnn. James Staatlect whom tits'? hoped to have the pleasure and ad.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

The voting papers for this annual election were collected on Wednesday and counted at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. F. H. Gossage was the returning officer, and he was assisted in his duties by Mr. Oppenheim (clerk), Mr. Craik (assistant clerk), Mr. S. Hoyle (accountant), and a number of counters. The contest had evoked considerable interest, and the slips issued half-hourly from noon showing the state of the poll, were eagerly scanned. At four o'clock the Returning Officer declared the result as follows : Brouchemite 457 Carr01l *Cook 1,458 Gerrard 1,243 *tionghton 1,745 *Mid wood *Owens Singleton Smith 1,221 *Timmis 2,383 Williamson The five against whom an asterisk appears were de- clared elected and are all the nominees of tile Owners and Occupiers Association. A vote of thanks was ac- corded to the Returning Officer on the motion of Major Wareing, seconded by Mr. Carroll, and in reply Mr. Gossage said this would be the last election for members lof the Local Board as it was certain the charter of in. corporation would be granted shortly.

COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION AT WIDNES. The election to fill the vacancy created in Widnes South Division through the election of Mr. T. Snape to the Aldermanic Bench took place on Saturday. The candidates were Mr. H. Wade Deacon (Liberal), and Mr. G. H. Sayce (Conserva- tive), and to judge by the activity displayed both sides were in earnest. The polling station was at Waterloo-road National Schools, where there were four polling booths in charge of Messrs. C. H. Lewin, J. W. Knowles, T. J. Peters, and G. H. Denby as presiding officers. A considerable number of conveyances were used by both parties. though it was apparent that the majority were in use for Mr. Deacon. There was veay little excitement throughout the day, but as eight o'clock drew near, the time for closing the poi% the streets become =very thronged and a crowd ot several thousands gathered in front of the Town Hall to await the result. At 9,15, Mr. F. H. Gossage the returning officer announced the result as fol- lows :—Deacon, 1,297; Sayce 335; majority 962. The declaration was received with loud cheering which was repeated when Mr. Stuart Deacon ap- pearedon the balcony to thank the eleetors in the name of his brother who was confined to his resi- dence with influenza. The usual vote of thank was passed to the returning officer for the Impartial manner in which he had conducted the contest.

James Burns, of Chadsmoor, and James Davies, Had- nestord. were assisting on Wednesday night to put out a gob fire at Erst Cannock Colliery when they were sent into some old workings to close the doors. As they did not return search was made, and their dead bodies were discovered, they having been killed by the poisonous atmosphere arising from the fire.
THE TORIES AND THE REPLY POST
CARD.
The Tories of Warrington are trying it on in Rood time. The following is a copy of Reply Post Card sent, amongst others, to Mr. R, Storey, of MO, Or- ford-lane :

div.head: ORFORD WARD.
div.p: ORFORD WARD.

Dew Sir, May I ask you ass favour if you are willing to sup- port the Conservative and Unionist Cause, and if I may rely upon your vote in favour of MR. ROBERT PIERPOINT at the approaching General Election ? Will you simply put" Yes "or " No" on the attached Post Card and post it to me at your early convenience. And much oblige, Yours faithfully GEORGE Y. BOLTON. Chairman of the Ward. 6492
THE ANSWER. Mr. Storey answers with rhyme and reason as follows:— Dear Mr. Editor, you see This Tory card was sent to in., From Tory Bolton of Orford Lane, "Who wants a vote," and he'll be fain!

But let us see if we can agree, If I vote for Pierpoint will he veto for rue "One man, one vote," I do demand; For paying .M.P.'s I firmly stand ; And also reform of our bad land laws; Mine rents and royalties, a great cause Of our bad trade, must be amended; And Home Rule strongly recommended. Would Mr. Pierpoint vote for these, If made M.P. ? His answer please?

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Rank rate of discount has been reduced from 3 to 2fi per cent. At Bristol. on Thursday. a Miss Dyer recovered £5OO damages against Mr. John S. Hare for breach of promise of:marriage. Mr. Adalbert Russell Withney,an American millionaire, is under arrest at Berlin on a charge of committing some scandalous offences.

A disastrous boiler explosion occurred on Monday, at Mr. F. Maston's bleach works, Hill Mill, Bolton. The damage is estimated at some thousands. Mr. W. IL Lever, of Port Sunlight, on Moaday con- sented to contest Birkenhead in the Liberal interest at the next election, if approved of by the " 300." A Sheriff's jury at Liverpool on Tuesday awarded £250 damages to Emma Lowry in an action for breach of promise brought against James Arthur Clayton, farmer, Aintree.

Sensational rumours regarding the safety of Lord Headley, who was last heard of while conducting an expedition through Mashonaland, are in circulation in Ireland. Lloyd's agent at Hamburg states that the British bar- que Crato sank whilst being towed into dock, on Thurs- day, and about 15 ram were drowned. The Crato belonged to London. The Imperial firman of investiture from the Sultan reached Alexandria on Monday, and a salute was fired by the warships in the harbour. The bearer of th e firman left for Cairo by special train. The barracks on the construction line of the Nicaragua Canal are reported to have been maliciously set on fire, and the shops, English Church, and mission houses were destroyed. Two persons perished in the flames. On Thursday morning, Richard Bromley, quarryman at Porthywaen, quarrelled with his wife, and afterwards cut the throats of three of his children, one of whom succumbed to the injuries. Bromley also cut his own throat.

Fire broke out on Monday in the corn/ming-room of Messrs. Eyre and Spottiswonde, Government printers, New-st., London, and the premises were practically gutted. Some dwelling-houses adjoining were partially destroyed. The folly of playing with firearms was sadly illustrated on Wednesday at Stockton-on-Tees. Messrs. Rupert Cooke, an engineer's wife, was entering the house when her son, aged 11, who was playing with an old gun, accidentally shot het dead. An extensive fire broke out in New Orleans late on Sunday night, its ravages not being checked until six blocks of buildings were destroyed. The damage is estimated at 4,000,000d015., and the insurance will amount to 3,500,000d015. At the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, John Hart, aged 35, a labourer, who had pleaded guilty to stealing from the London and Westminster Bank, Loth- bury, a box containing securities of the value of £20,000, was sentenced to 12 maths' hard labour. Mr. Henry Irving, giving evidence, on Monday, before Mr. Plunkett's Select Committee of the House of Com- mons regarding theatre and music hall licenses said he was strongly opposed to licenses for the performance of stage plays being given to music .halls, which he de- scribed as really taverns which had obtained licenses for music and dancing.

MTSTBUIOt7S DISAPPHARINCII. On Monday week, Thomas Rigby, a middle-aged widower, living at Billinge, came to St. Helens, and at night was with a man named Hooton in the Ship Inn. Blackbrook. To go to Bißinge he would proceed along the canal side and past Carr Mill dam. Baotou missed him, and nothing more has been heard or seen of him. It is feared he has got into the dam, which is a great depth.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT STUETTON. Mr. Wonley held an inquest at the Cat and Lion. Stretton, on Monday, on the body of Oliver Miller, three years of age, the son of John Miller, a brick- setter's labourer, living in Lower Stretton. It ap- peared from the evidence that the child was left in the house in charge of a sister seven years of age, the mother having gone into the fields to work and the father being at his usual employment. On Fri- day, Mary Ann Miller was lighting the fire, when she accidentally set the deceased s clothes on fire. The little one in his fear and agony ran into the lane, where the dames were extinguished by several neighbours, but the deceased had been so badly burnt that he died on the following day. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that in pursuance of the Provisions of the Warrington Improvement and I Market Act. 1854, the Towns Improvement Clauses Act, 1847. incorporated therewith, and the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879, the Corporation did previous to tke Fifth day of April, 1892, cause an estimate to be prepared of the money required for the several purposes, in respect of which they are authorized to lay an IMPROVE- MENT RATE and a GENERAL SEWERS RATE for the said Borough, showing the several particulars required by the said Acts to be shown thereby, and the same were approved by the Corporation, at a Meeting of the Council on the Filth day of April, 1892, and have been duly entered in the Rate Books. And Notice is hereby further Given, that it is in- tended at a Meeting of the Finance Committee appointed by the said Corporation, to be held at the Town Hall in the said Borough. on Monday, the Eleventh day of April instant, at Three o'clock in the afternoon, to make an Improvement Rate and • General Sewers Rate for the said Borough accordingly; and in the meantime the statements required by the afore- said Acts of the proposed Rates are deposited for inspection by the Ratepayers at the Office of the Borough Treasurer, Town Hall, aforesaid, at which place the said statements and the Rates, Immediately after the same are made, will be open to the inspection of any person interested or rated in such rates at all reasonable times. Dated this Sixth day of April. 1892. J. LYON WHITTLE, Town Clerk.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS. L/DINS IND GENTLEMEN,-04 behalf of the five success- ful candidates—Messrs. COOK. HOUGIITON, MIDWCOD, OWENS, and TIMMIS,—We beg to thank you most sincerely for the support accorded to the above named gentle- men. By returning them with such a sweeprng majority. you may emphatically declare your intention of keeping up the status of the Hoed, and shown your appreciation of the policy pursued by that body In the past. Signed on behalf of the Candidates' Committee, JNO. W. WARNING. Chairman.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION, 1852. LADIES awn GENTLEMEN,—I sincerely thank those who have supported me in my uphill fight. Although not successful now, the time will shortly arrive when the workingman can say who shall or who shall no represent him. The accumulative vote Is an obstacle we have been unable to overcome, but when we receive our charter of incorporation each voter will be on an equal footing with those who now have several votes at their disposal. INDo not be disheartened, but prepare for the &anted In November, Tours truly, JOHN WILLIAMSON.

A. WIDNES WARRANT FOR DEEMING'S ARREST. We are informed that the Public Prosecutor will next Monday apply at the Widnes Police Court for a warrant for the apprehension of the man Deeming, which is to be served on the prisoner if necessary in Australia. • PENKETH MUSICA.L LECTURB AT PENKETH. On Monday evening a musical lecture, entitled "An Evening with Mendelssohn„' was delivered at the Friends' School, Penketh, by the Rev. E. Moore. The musical illustrations were supplied by Mrs. Varley (pianoforte), Mr. R. H. Pearson (violin), and Mr. Henry Bond (violoncello). The lecture room was well filled with a select audience. go- FRODSHAM. A PUBLICAN CRAMISD WITN ASSAULY.—On Wednesday Thomas Morris, licensee of the Volunteer Inn, Frodsham, was brought before Mr. Thomas, under a warrant charg- ing him with having assaulted his wife, Harriet Morris, on the previous day. Defendant was bound over to keep the peace, in his own surety of £lo,and two sureties of £5 each. ALLEGHD SYSTEMATIC FRAUDS.—OR Wednesday morn- ing, at the Frodsham Police Court, before Mr. Thomas, a labourer, named James Turner, of Newtown, Frods- ham, was charged with obtaining money by false pre- tences. It was stated that the prisoner had for some time been carrying on systematic kinds of fraud by means of a letter, purporting to be signed by a late em- ployer. A remand was granted. WAYWARDHN FOR FRODSRAM LORDSHIP.—Tho poll de- manded at the recent vestry meeting, in the appointment of waywarden for the township, took place in the Grammar' School, Overton, on Saturday, Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., being the returning officer. The following number of votes were recorded fur the two candidates for the post :—Mr. James Percival, Godscroft, near Frod- sham, 10E1 ; Mr. J. H. Hargreaves, Overton, 19. Mr. Percival was, therefore, elected waywarden for the town- ship.
